Think about what's sitting in your inbox and Drive right now. Client contracts and invoices. Project specs under NDA. Staging credentials a client emailed you. That API key or password you meant to delete.

For most developers and freelancers, all of it lives in Google Workspace or Microsoft 365. Both are excellent tools, and both encrypt your data in transit and at rest. But in their standard setup, the provider holds the encryption keys, which means your provider (and the integrated apps and AI features connected to it) can access what's inside.

Proton Workspace takes a different approach: the same everyday tools, with encryption designed so that not even Proton can read your data.

Here's how the three compare, what each does best, and which makes the most sense for how you work.

Google and Microsoft are built around ecosystem integration. Proton is built around keeping your data yours, without sacrificing productivity tools.

Google Workspace is the go-to suite for startups, agencies and freelancers, and for good reason. Gmail, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Calendar and Meet work together seamlessly, and several people can edit the same file in real time without emailing versions back and forth.

Google encrypts data at rest and in transit, and offers client-side encryption on eligible editions. But that extra layer requires higher-tier plans and configuration, so in the default experience Google holds the keys. A password manager and VPN aren't part of the suite.

Best for: Teams whose top priorities are real-time collaboration and third-party integrations.

If your work runs on Word, Excel and Outlook, Microsoft 365 needs little introduction. Business Standard includes full desktop apps, and Excel remains the benchmark for heavy spreadsheet work.

That breadth comes with complexity. Licensing, permissions and device management can eat into time a small team or solo developer would rather spend shipping. And like Google, Microsoft's everyday productivity experience isn't built around end-to-end encryption, while Copilot and advanced security features add cost.

Best for: Businesses built on desktop Office apps and established Microsoft workflows.

Everything is managed from one admin console, with one bill.

This is the core difference. Proton uses zero-access encryption: your data is encrypted before it reaches Proton's servers, and Proton never holds the keys. Proton can't read your data. Not won't. Can't.

The honest trade-offs: Proton Docs and Sheets cover core editing and collaboration, not every advanced Excel feature. There's no presentation app yet, and the third-party integration ecosystem is smaller than Google's or Microsoft's.

The headline prices are close. The real cost isn't:

Proton Workspace covers business email, 1 TB of encrypted storage, docs, sheets, video calls, a password manager and a VPN. That's one bill instead of three.

Need more? Workspace Premium and adds 3 TB of storage per user, 20 custom domains, meetings for up to 250 participants, Lumo private AI and email data retention policies for only $7 more per month. Both plans include a 14-day free trial, and annual plans are currently up to 20% off.

Choose Google Workspace if your team lives in real-time collaboration and relies heavily on Google's integration ecosystem.

Choose Microsoft 365 if your work depends on desktop Excel, PowerPoint and established Microsoft workflows.

Less than you might expect. Proton's Easy Switch tool imports email, contacts and calendars from Google Workspace and other providers, and you keep your custom domain, so clients won't notice a thing. Smaller teams can migrate on their own, and Proton's business team supports larger moves.

Moving from Microsoft 365? Check the migration options for each data type rather than assuming every workflow transfers automatically.

Is Proton Workspace a good alternative to Google Workspace for developers?

Can Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 read my email and files?

By default, yes. Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 hold the encryption keys, and their default terms give them access to your data.

No. Zero-access encryption means Proton never holds the keys to your stored data. Emails between Proton users are end-to-end encrypted automatically, and you can send password-protected encrypted emails to anyone.

Yes. Proton's apps are open source and independently audited.

Can I use Proton Mail with my existing email client?

Yes. Proton Mail Bridge connects Outlook, Apple Mail and Thunderbird.

Does Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 use my data to train AI?

It can. If your plan allows Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 to hold the encryption keys, they can access your data and use it to train their integrated AI models.

No. Proton can't read your data, so it can't use it for AI training.

Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 are mature, capable platforms, and if your work depends on advanced Excel or a deep web of Google integrations, there's a good case for using them.

But if you're a freelancer or a developer or running a small team, Proton Workspace is the stronger choice. You get the same core tools for less money, a password manager and VPN you'd otherwise pay for separately, and encryption that keeps client data, code and credentials readable only by you.

#10458. Amazon’s new Ring cameras are mounted to roving robots, including $250 Drone Cam

Amazon’s Ring brand is today launching a new “Robotics” division that will start with two offerings – a $250 Ring Drone Cam and a $1,000 Rover Cam.

Indoor cameras can be invaluable for securing your home, but also just in keeping an eye on what’s going on when you’re not home. To that end, Ring has been working on cameras that can be sent around the home remotely, and they’re finally launching early next year.

Ring first showed off its Drone Cam in 2020, but never actually brought the product to market. That changes in January of next year, when the Ring Drone Cam will be available for $249.99. The camera, Amazon expains, is “a flying indoor security camera that goes where you need it, when you need it, and stays docked and out of sight when you don’t.” You can set flight routes on a schedule, have the drone automatically investigate tripped sensors in your Ring system, and more. The camera is only active when the drone is in flight, and it’s emphasized that the drone is not “quiet,” it’s “meant to be seen and heard.”

The other robot Amazon’s Ring is launching is the Rover Cam, which is built on the back of Amazon Astro. It has a telescoping camera and rolls around your home on “scheduled patrols” as well as being able to automatically investigate tripped sensors. It also features two-way audio and a built-in siren to deter intruders from an area, while also features continuous 4K recording.

Ring is mainly pitching this one for businesses, and it costs $999.99 with pre-orders open now ahead of a December 16 release date.

The King 95 3D is a solid, premium-class mid-tower with three tempered-glass panels for panoramic views inside. The seven included Link fans on the Pro version deliver enough airflow and RGB bling, but can get noisy at full speed. For $119 or $199 for the Pro, it’s an excellent update from the original King 95.

Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

PC case, cooling, and PSU maker Montech is celebrating its 10th anniversary this year and has released a new flagship ATX chassis, the King 95 3D and 3D Pro. Like the previous King 95, the 3D version keeps the signature 15-degree curved-glass panoramic front panel and adds a top glass panel, giving you a third window and a unique aesthetic for viewing your build. An integrated, contoured ARGB strip follows the chassis's smooth lines, making it look every bit the king of the castle.

Inside, the large mid-tower chassis supports multiple radiators (though only one 360mm), large graphics cards (plus integrated adjustable GPU support), CPU air coolers, and spots for 2.5- and 3.5-inch drives. However, it doesn't support E-ATX motherboards. The King 95 3D supports rear-connect motherboards and has ample room for cable routing and management. The front aluminum panel IO runs vertically, as with previous King cases, and includes a fast USB 3.2 Gen2x2 (20 Gbps) Type-C port. Overall, it has everything you want in a premium chassis. The uncommon three-panel view into your PC is a great way to show off your rig.

The King 95 3D is available for an inexpensive (at least for curved glass) $119.90 if you want to select your own fans. The 3D Pro includes seven pre-installed LINK Fan INF 120 fans for builders who want a more coordinated look out of the box, plus it includes the Lumi hub (a dedicated fan controller), for $199.90. We have the 3D Pro version in our lab and ran the case through thermal and noise testing in its out-of-the-box configuration to show how it performs compared to others. Will it make our best PC cases list? It has a chance. But before we get into the details, here are the case's specifications from Montech.

21 x 21 x 18.8 x 11.8-inches (534 x 480 x 300mm)

Top - 3x120Front - N/ABottom - 3x120mmSide: - 2x120mmRear - 2x120mm

(5) Link Fan INF 120 (Reverse blades, side/bottom)(2) Link Fan INF 120 (rear)

Front - N/ATop - 120/240/360mmSide - 120/240mmRear - 120mm

Great internal views, 7x pre-installed fans (Pro version), integrated GPU support, adjustable angle bottom fans

King 95 3D - $119.90 (w/o fans)King 95 3D Pro - $199.90 (w/7 pre-installed fans)

From the outside, the King 95 3D Pro looks the part of its royal name. That signature curve and three panes of glass offer a panoramic view inside your case like few others, letting you show off your PC from even more angles. It also features a frosted, continuous LED strip running along the tiered top, right side, and bottom, adding some tasteful bling to the chassis. If you get the Pro version with the seven fans, it’s an RGB light show inside which could be polarizing. I do wish there were an option for preinstalled non-RGB fans, since the seven included ones and the infinity mirror styling may not be for everyone. Still, the curved front corner and clean lines really cement the King 95 3D as one of the better-looking panoramic cases on the market.

Up front, the removable curved glass corner with a smoked tint sets it apart from most others. On the right, the front IO panel runs vertically, with the power button on top and the LED on/off button below. It has three USB ports: one 3.2 Gen2x2 (20 Gbps) Type-C and two USB 3.2 Gen1 (5 Gbps) Type-A ports. Finally, it has a 3.5mm audio jack. That continuous 118-LED strip is visible from the front, running along the top, down the right edge, and along the bottom edge. I’m not a fan of a lot of RGB, but this implementation is tasteful. You can control this lighting through the motherboard software or Montech's Lumi software, which lets you fully customize the fans and RGB strip.

The main window panel also uses a smoke-colored tint, with Montech branding in the upper-right corner, and it's secured to the frame by two captive thumbscrews on the back. To remove it, loosen the thumbscrews, slide the panel back, pull from the top, then lift it out of the slots. Easy. I have to say, the biggest problem with all this glass is keeping it pristine and fingerprint-free.The other (metal) side panel, behind the motherboard, slots into the frame and is secured the same way. It has filtered venting along the top and side for the fans/radiator locations, plus another area for airflow near the power supply and drive mounting locations. In the middle is a gold placard with Montech King 95 3D 10th anniversary badging. Note: The dust filters on this panel aren't removable, so you’ll need to remove the whole panel to clean things up.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

At the top, we get a better look at the third windowed panel, letting observers peer into the case from a different angle rather than straight on or from the front. We can also see the tiered top and part of the long RGB strip. Taking this panel off isn’t as simple as the rest. Yes, it’s also secured by two captive thumbscrews on the back, but to remove it, you’ll need to open the main window panel to expose a retaining screw, remove it, then loosen the back thumbscrews and slide it to the rear. After you remove the top glass, you can remove the upper and side retaining screws to take it out. When building, I didn’t find this necessary, but it’s good to know you can take it apart if needed.

Looking at the case from behind, one of the first things I noticed was the vertical PSU mounting location on the left. This space supports up to 220mm power supplies, which is all but the largest on the market. On the right, we see space for two 120mm fans, the motherboard I/O, and seven horizontal expansion slots. Unfortunately, Montech says the King 95 3D does not support vertical GPUs.

Underneath the case, there isn’t a lot going on. We get a better look at the four short rubber-bottom ‘feet’ and the removable dust filter. Montech put on its thinking cap and designed the dust filter to slide out from the front, so chances are you won’t have to move your heavy case to clean it.

Inside, the case uses a dual-chamber design, with the power supply and all wires hidden behind the motherboard tray. At the bottom, we see three Link Fan INF 120s (reverse blade) along with the mirror finish. The magnetically linked, daisy-chainable fans run up to 2,300 RPM (2,200 RPM on the reverse blade), pushing between 65-67 CFM with a maximum rating of 32dBA (29 dBA on the standard blade). A single Link Fan INF 120 costs $19.90, while a 3-pack (with Lumi Hub) is $64.90. If you do the math for seven fans and the Lumi Hub, it’s cheaper to buy them with the case rather than separately.

When powered on, the mirrored sides become an infinity panel, and with all seven matching, it creates a consistent view across the build. The bottom fan bracket is adjustable, with three positions (8 degrees). We left it down during testing, but with it up, you can focus more air towards the GPU and show off whatever fans you put in the space.

The motherboard tray has plenty of cutouts to access the back of the motherboard for easy installation/removal of air coolers or AIO/custom water-cooling blocks. The case also supports rear-connect ecosystems, including Asus BTF, Gigabyte Stealth, and MSI Project Zero boards. Grommets surround the motherboard tray and are in ideal locations, but like most, they pull out easily when you try to route cables, especially those with larger connectors. I wish all case vendors would secure these better, since they're a pain to reinstall, especially when the case is full of cables.Up top, we can see the huge gap above the motherboard tray for more fans and radiators. The case cooled just fine with the seven included fans and our air cooler, though GPU temps ran a bit warmer in our noise-normalized testing. That top gap is begging to be filled with fans, even if only for aesthetics. If you plan to use an AIO cooler, this isn’t a problem, since the radiator/fans will fill the space.

From the front, you can see the two Link INF 120mm fans and, at the bottom, the tool-less, adjustable GPU support strut. The back has space to mount two 120mm fans or one 120mm radiator. You can also see the seven horizontal expansion slots held in by thumbnail screws.

Inside, the top of the case above the motherboard space fits up to three 120mm fans or a 360mm radiator. The space is offset back from the motherboard tray, which is a boon for cable management. Normally, there’s barely any room to route the EPS cables, but here there's plenty. Just note that if your build uses air cooling, you will need to fill that area with fans to make it look good. Otherwise, it’s just a blank open space above the motherboard.

On the rear side of the chassis, we get a good look at the space behind the motherboard tray and the fan baffles. There’s plenty of room to route cables, and Montech has multiple pre-installed Velcro straps for cable routing. Even with the power supply installed, there’s plenty of room underneath it to stash excess cables.

At the bottom, we see a simple ARGB hub that consolidates the three different ARGB cables from the fans into one header to control all of them. Montech also includes a magnetic Lumi fan/RGB hub (which supports up to 13 Link Fans total) with both the Pro and non-Pro variants. Oddly, it comes loose/uninstalled on the Pro, but installed on the non-Pro. The box in the lower-right holds one 3.5-inch HDD and a single 2.5-inch drive. The second 2.5-inch drive mounts in the other location at the bottom left, next to the side fans.

We do like the look of the King 95 3D Pro case in black, and I bet it looks great in white with an all-white build too. The curved glass and 3-panel panoramic interior views are great for anyone who’d like to show off their now-ridiculously expensive parts. The included Link Fan INF 120 fans work well and run relatively quietly. If there’s an aesthetic drawback, it's that I’m not a huge fan of all the RGB and infinity mirrors on the pre-installed fans. It’s a lot, and it makes me yearn for an option with preinstalled fans and no RGB. Of course, you can turn them off in the software, or buy the non-Pro and choose whichever fans fit your build.

Samsung is working on a long overdue redesign for its Galaxy S27 series and, this week, we’re getting a fresh look.

ASRock has rolled out a new firmware update for its Radeon RX 7000-series graphics cards. The latest VBIOS version 1.0.6 appears to be a follow-up to the previous 1.0.5 release. According to community reports, that older version was bricking some of the company's Radeon RX 7900 XT and RX 7900 XTX graphics cards. The new update has now quietly made its way to the ASRock official website, although the company has not published a changelog or provided any details on what the new update addresses.

Last month, AMD released a VBIOS patch for Radeon RX 7000-series graphics cards to address potential security vulnerabilities. While the company did not disclose any technical details about the vulnerabilities, it assured gamers that there had been no reports of them being exploited. According to a statement shared with ComputerBase, the company provided the following rationale for the update:

"AMD is releasing a firmware update as part of our usual approach to address potential security vulnerabilities. These corrections are already made available before the public announcement to give customers time to update their firmware. As a best practice, we recommend that users update the firmware of their graphics cards as soon as they are provided by the respective GPU manufacturer. There are no reports of exploiting these security vulnerabilities in practice."

ASRock subsequently listed the 1.0.5 VBIOS update for 10 graphics card models, spanning its Radeon RX 7600 XT, RX 7700 XT, RX 7800 XT, RX 7900 XT, and RX 7900 XTX families. However, several Radeon RX 7900 XT and RX 7900 XTX owners reported that their systems failed to boot after installing the firmware. Some lucky users were able to use external EEPROM programmers to recover their cards. Although ASRock has since removed the 1.0.5 update from its website, it has yet to provide clarity on what caused the failures or confirm whether the newly released VBIOS addresses the issue.

There are also unanswered questions around how ASRock plans to help customers who have already been affected. According to reports shared with VideoCardz, a user in Japan received a confirmation from ASRock that the failed update would be covered under warranty. However, another owner in Europe was reportedly directed to seek warranty service despite having an out-of-warranty graphics card. This essentially leaves affected owners uncertain of whether they will receive free repairs or replacements.

Additionally, the lack of a changelog or an official statement, along with the new firmware version, makes it difficult for users to determine whether installing the replacement firmware is safe. We can only hope that ASRock provides some clarity around what version 1.06

#10452. An expert in espionage on spies, honeypots, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang

Nvidia announced early Thursday morning that CEO Jensen Huang had resigned from the company. The updates come after reports that Huang had been having affairs with an alleged Chinese spy, as well as an executive who reported to him at the company. The scandal has spurred myriad national security concerns and sent Nvidia stock tumbling.

For the chipmaker—which sources some 80% of the world’s GPUs—Huang’s exit marks the loss of an executive who led the company through an AI craze and to record profits. But for the United States, and the tech industry more broadly, the scandal raises concerns about ongoing attempts by spies to steal valuable intellectual property and compromise the country’s leading technology executives.

“I can vouch for the lack of concern by senior executives about such matters,” Matt Brazil, an expert in espionage now writing about the topic and a former U.S. Army officer, corporate security investigator, and expert control official, told Fast Company. “They will freely spend money to increase revenue but are far less enthusiastic about outlays to protect revenues, reduce losses, or promote security awareness.”

Brazil, who is also a senior fellow at the Jamestown Foundation, a global analysis firm, emailed with Fast Company from Melbourne, Australia about the prevalence of honeypot schemes, the threat of espionage to tech companies, and what steps boards take to investigate their top executives. 

This email interview has been edited for length. 

How common are these kinds of honeypot schemes, particularly those backed by the Chinese government and targeting American tech executives?

Unfortunately, they may be very common. For example, there are parallels in this case with the problem from a decade ago involving the Chinese agent—or officer—Christine Fang.  Ms. Fang targeted California and other politicians and used sexual exploitation to gather information and build influence. However, this case regarding [Alice Huang, the leader of Singapore-based Megaspeed and alleged spy for the Chinese government] was potentially far more successful because of who Jensen Huang is, what he knows, his access to technology, and his connections, including in Silicon Valley and with the White House.

What do you imagine the target was: Nvidia intellectual property, classified intel from the Trump administration, or a voice in Washington in favor of loosening chip restrictions? Something else?

The target could be all of the above. If Ms. Huang had access to Jensen’s devices during an overnight stay, all of the above could have been compromised because there is no telling what was on his phone and laptop hard drive. A national-level security agency could have given her devices to quickly copy a hard drive in the time it takes for Jensen to be in the shower. As someone who regularly texted the president, his devices could have practically anything because of Mr. Trump’s habit of sharing sensitive information with those he trusts.   

What kind of training and oversight do tech executives have to prevent this kind of stuff?

Very little unless there is leadership from the top to spend the money and time needed to train executives. From nearly two decades in international business, I can vouch for the lack of concern by senior executives about such matters. They will freely spend money to increase revenue but are far less enthusiastic about outlays to protect revenues, reduce losses, or promote security awareness. They are very conservative about thorough background investigations, for example, except for a few “positions of trust” that generally are connected to revenue (i.e. the CFO). The people who handle technology and operations tend to be trusted until they violate the company’s code of conduct.

Are you warned about honeypots and other similar espionage schemes when you get security clearance? Is this something company boards require—or should require?

Yes, people in government are trained about this threat. Company boards need to consider a paradigm change in their priorities and requirements of management on these issues. More training is needed, more monitoring of behavior, and more resources should be allocated to corporate security departments. There is a tendency to view security and background checks as “cost centers,” versus revenue centers such as manufacturing, sales, design, and marketing. That is the mentality that has helped lead us all to this moment.

Does Nvidia’s market concentration—the company might have as much as 80% of the GPU market—make the risks associated with these kinds of honeypot schemes worse? 

Yes, just because of who and what they are.

#10450. Who is Colette Kress? Meet the new interim CEO of one of the world’s most powerful companies

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday morning following revelations of his affair with an alleged Chinese spy, and the subsequent reporting that he had also been in an extramarital relationship with another company executive.

Huang will be replaced by Colette Kress as interim CEO, who is currently Nvidia’s executive vice president and CFO. Here’s what to know about the new interim chief:

How long will Colette Kress remain in the interim role?

Kress will serve as CEO and CFO until a permanent successor for Huang has been named, a company announcement reads.

Nvidia’s board is now “initiating a search” for a permanent CEO, “and will consider internal and external candidates.”

The company did not give a timeline for how long it anticipates its search for a new CEO will take.

Who is Colette Kress?

Kress has held the title of executive vice president and CFO since she joined Nvidia in 2013. Prior to that, she held various finance roles at tech companies for the preceding 25 years, including stretches at Cisco, Microsoft, and Texas Instruments. 

She earned her bachelor’s degree at the University of Arizona, and an MBA from SMU. 

Kress has worked closely with the outgoing boss

Over the past 13 years, Kress has reportedly worked closely with Huang as Nvidia grew from a relatively small tech company into a behemoth, with a market cap larger, at times, than Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, and others. 

Kress’s background in finance and broader business operations will set her apart from Huang, an electrical engineer by trade. 

Perhaps where she has truly shined in recent years is in her ability to explain to Wall Street and investors just what, exactly, was happening with Nvidia as it transitioned from a smaller player in the chipmaking industry and grew to monumental heights in recent years largely due to the boom in artificial intelligence.

Nvidia’s powerful graphics processing units (GPUs) have been the backbone of the technology behind the AI revolution.   

Kress was selected by Huang to become Nvidia’s CFO after a two-year search, and according to reporting from The New York Times, was initially encouraged to take the job at Nvidia at the behest of her children, who were video game fans. 

In 2025, she was one of a handful of CFOs to become a billionaire, according to Bloomberg’s Billionaires Index.

#10449. How Jensen Huang’s personal brand boomeranged

Few CEOs have had as distinct a public image as Nvidia founder Jensen Huang. The leather jackets, the social media cameos resulting from his street-food enthusiasm, the theatrical optimism about an AI future powered in part by his company’s chips. For years, Huang’s personal brand has been effective and winning.

But now, of course, the revelation of an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy, and another with a subordinate, has thrown 63-year-old Huang’s reputation into a tailspin, and ultimately cost him his job, as he resigned under pressure from Nvidia’s board. As for that potent personal brand—it may well have worked against him.

Huang isn’t the first business figure to cultivate a high-flying public image, only to see it crash back to reality. Elon Musk rode a quirky mad genius vibe into hosting SNL in 2021; today his reputation is, let’s say, mixed. Elizabeth Holmes landed on magazine covers as an innovator with a turtleneck and a husky voice; today she is in prison. The AI boom seems particularly fueled by larger-than-life characters, and figures like OpenAI chief Sam Altman and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei have already seen their demigod status undermined.

But the arc of The Brand Called Jensen Huang stands out. Just a few years ago, Huang’s public profile was modest. Born in Taiwan, Huang was sent to a boarding school in the U.S. at age 9. He went on to work in Silicon Valley as a chip designer, and co-founded Nvidia in 1993. Only in the past couple of years, as AI took off, have its industry-leading chips become widely coveted, making Nvidia a household name—and Huang a public figure.

Despite crafting his personal story around the relatable attributes of hard work and fear of failure, Huang has become a hugely powerful presence in the AI debate. Yes, he has a regular-guy taste for street food and mingling with fans, but in Taiwan, he’s reportedly treated as a borderline pop star, attracting autograph- and selfie-seekers.

Then there were the leather jackets. Huang has reportedly worn a black leather jacket and T-shirt for public events for more than a decade, and today owns at least 30. A “Jensen Jacket” designed by Tom Ford and signed (and worn) by Huang sold through Sotheby’s in July for $960,000 (over its $40,000–60,000 estimate). 

The catalog entry described the item as “an iconic garment associated with some of the most consequential moments in modern technology.” Noting that Huang wore such jackets for product launches and street corner meals, Sotheby’s declared: “This is not only a jacket. It is the uniform of a ‘first believer’; a symbol of his leadership style embodying authenticity, ingenuity, persistence, courage and joy. It has become a symbol for the vision at the forefront of the AI revolution.”

Much of this public persona has boomeranged. Huang’s joie de vivre now feels cavalier, his breezy optimism naïve. And the leather jacket now reads as some sort of midlife-crises symbol. While the likes of High Snobiety credits Huang for coming across as “someone with drip,” unlike “the sartorially confused Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg,” the street-fashion site also cautioned, in the wake of the Huang scandals, that even the most studiously orchestrated public image is “brittle,” and “attaching yourself to a piece of clothing so tied to rebelliousness is a gamble when things go sideways.”

In an ironic but telling twist, an AI-faked image of Huang in a particularly ostentatious studded Saint Laurent/Hedi Slimane jacket went viral just as Nvidia’s board was considering his fate. Aside from illustrating that even AI’s greatest champions are subject to the technology’s abuse, the image turned Huang’s public brand inside out, with the leather jacket signaling ostentatious indifference.

Now that Huang has resigned, it’s unclear what his post-Nvidia fate may turn out to be. But that personal brand that served him so well has become a liability. We’ll never see his leather jackets the same way again.

#10445. When a Walmart disappears, here’s what happens to nearby stores. It’s not what you’d expect

Shoppers often greet the closure of a Walmart with dismay, while competitors find cause to celebrate.

Among critics of the big-box behemoth, a long-held assumption is that once a Walmart disappears, shoppers seeking groceries, household goods, meals and services will flow to businesses down the road.

But what if the economic downside of a closure is bigger?

We are marketing scholars who have studied dozens of Walmart closures in the United States. We found that nearby stores saw a slump in both monthly shopper traffic and sales revenue by roughly a quarter in contrast to comparable stores near Walmart locations that remained open. Our sample covered 39 Walmart stores that closed across 20 states from 2019 to 2026.

This finding suggests a large retailer can play two roles at once. Walmart competes with neighboring businesses for shopper visits and spending. But it can also act as an anchor, giving people a reason to travel to a shopping area in the first place. When that anchor disappears, the loss of shared shopper traffic can outweigh the benefit of having one less competitor.

The benefits of an anchor

Our finding underscores that retailers don’t operate as isolated dots on a map. Shoppers often decide where to go before deciding which stores they’ll visit once they get there. A trip to Walmart can generate a stop at a nearby restaurant, pharmacy, salon, specialty retailer or service business.

Economists call this kind of benefit an agglomeration effect: Businesses can gain from being near other businesses because the location itself attracts shoppers. Shopping center owners have long recognized this logic by using prominent stores to anchor a mix of tenants.

Other researchers have found that Walmart’s entry into a shopping area causes sales in nearby existing stores to drop. But these shops can adjust their product assortment, prices and promotions to mitigate this effect, follow-up studies suggest. What has not been studied until now is what happens when a Walmart store – or any other anchor store – closes.

A Walmart closure creates a tug-of-war between two forces, we argue. Competitive relief helps nearby businesses because a formidable rival is gone. But agglomeration loss hurts them because fewer shoppers have a reason to visit the area.

This means a store can capture a larger share of local consumer demand after Walmart leaves and still end up worse off if the total pool of shoppers arriving in the area shrinks enough.

What happened after a Walmart closed

We combined closure dates with monthly store-level shopper traffic and spending data. For each closed Walmart, we identified nearby non-Walmart businesses and compared their post-closure performance with that of businesses near Walmarts that stayed open.

We discovered not just a sizable decline in both shopper traffic and sales revenue after closure but a worsening trend in both over time. Specifically, following a Walmart’s closure, nearby stores experienced a roughly 5% drop in the following month and 6% in the month thereafter. The decline keeps getting worse, reaching about 17% in the ninth month and 20% a year after the anchor store closes.

That parallel movement in traffic and sales matters. If nearby stores were simply selling less to the same number of shoppers, we would expect spending per visit to fall. Instead, what was also happening is that fewer shoppers visited nearby businesses after the anchor disappeared.

In short, competitive relief didn’t overcome the loss of traffic that would have been generated by trips to the anchor store. But not all nearby businesses were affected equally.

Stores that competed more directly with Walmart had better post-closure sales than noncompeting stores. That is what we would expect if competitive relief is real: Grocery stores and other close substitutes are better positioned to capture some of the displaced consumer demand.

Well-known brand stores also fared relatively better than unbranded businesses. A recognizable brand can give shoppers an independent reason to visit, reducing reliance on traffic generated by the nearby anchor. And stores surrounded by more outlets with its own brands also had more favorable post-closure sales.

Another important factor is digital reach. Not surprisingly, the more a business engages with customers online, the less it depends on people physically traveling to a cluster of stores. We found that stores with a higher share of revenue from online orders saw a less severe drop in sales after a Walmart closed.

These patterns suggest that managers have options and can act: Opening another location or expanding online sales can protect a retailer from an anchor closure.

Why a store closing can become a neighborhood shock

A large retailer decides whether to keep a store open based primarily on what makes sense for its own portfolio. But the surrounding businesses face a different calculation. A location that looks weak from the anchor retailer’s perspective can still drive valuable traffic to neighboring stores.

That creates what economists call an externality — a positive or negative effect of an economic activity that impacts other parties even though market prices don’t reflect it. In this case, some of the economic value produced by an anchor sits outside the anchor’s own sales and profits.

For neighboring businesses, the lesson is not to assume that a powerful competitor’s departure will create a windfall. Rather, managers need to know how many customers arrive because of the broader shopping destination, not merely how much their store’s products overlap with the anchor’s.

Meanwhile, commercial property owners should treat losing an anchor as more than risking an empty storefront. It can also hurt the rest of their portfolio by reducing consumer demand. Replacing the tenant quickly matters, but so does finding a replacement that can generate trips to the area.

Finally, local governments and economic development organizations need to understand that a major retail closure may affect businesses with no contractual relationship to the closed store. So their responses should extend beyond the vacant property itself — whether it’s speeding redevelopment, coordinating with local businesses and property owners to improve shoppers’ access, or helping create a new destination that restores shopper traffic.

Vivek Astvansh is an associate professor of quantitative marketing and computational data science at Binghamton University, State University of New York; Preetinder Kaur is assistant professor of marketing at the University of Guelph, and Pushpinder Gill is an assistant professor of marketing at Toronto Metropolitan University.

#10444. Prompt Management in TypeScript: LangSmith vs Git vs 3 Open-Source Registries

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Every prompt registry we tested can change a prompt in a running TypeScript app, roll it back, and give production and staging different versions. LangSmith's prompt hub, Langfuse, Phoenix and AcruxCore all passed those three tests. The real differences show up elsewhere: which template syntax each one accepts, how many npm packages it pulls in, how long a change takes to reach the app, and what happens when the registry is down.

We tested all of this with one small app and one prompt, which has a condition and a loop. Git files served as the baseline. Every number below comes from a recorded run.

Most teams start with prompts in code: a template string, or a .txt file next to the code that uses it. That works until a product manager wants to change one sentence, and the change has to wait for a full release.

A prompt registry moves the text out of the deploy. The app fetches the prompt by name and by a label such as production. You change which version the label points to, and the app picks up the new text without a deploy.

LangSmith's prompt hub is the best-known registry, but it is not the only one. Several of the LangSmith alternatives also manage prompts, and three of them are open source and self-hostable: Langfuse, Phoenix and AcruxCore. We covered how those tools handle tracing in Self-Hosted LangSmith Alternatives: 4 Tools Tested on One TypeScript Agent. This article covers prompts only.

Every tool got the same prompt, support-reply. Its template takes three variables: a customer name, a plan, and a list of help articles. It has one condition: a priority line appears only for premium customers. It also has one loop: one line per help article. In Jinja2 syntax, the template looks like this:

One help article contains the text Settings > Export. We included it on purpose, to catch any tool that HTML-escapes > into >.

Every tool then ran the same sequence from a TypeScript script:

Each tool used its own documented TypeScript SDK. The four registries passed all six steps. The rest of this article covers how each one got there, and what it cost.

Keeping prompts in the repository costs almost nothing. The template sits in prompts/support-reply.njk, and nunjucks, the JavaScript port of Jinja2, renders it:

The autoescape: false line matters. Our first version called nunjucks.renderString() directly, and the test failed. The default environment HTML-escapes its output, so Settings > Export reached the model as Settings > Export. Escaping is correct for web pages and wrong for prompts.

Git gives you full Jinja2, code review on every prompt change, and history in the same place as the code. What it can't do is change a prompt in a running app. Every edit, and every rollback, waits for a deploy.

LangSmith stores a prompt as a serialized LangChain object (ChatPromptTemplate), not as plain text. LangSmith's own documentation says you must use the LangChain npm package to pull prompts in TypeScript (Manage prompts programmatically). So a plain TypeScript app that uses the openai package still needs langchain and @langchain/core:

Those three packages installed 23 packages and 70 MB. Most of the size is @langchain/* (27 MB) and js-tiktoken (22 MB).

Templates. In TypeScript, LangChain accepts f-string and mustache templates. Mustache sections ({{#docs}}…{{/docs}}) handled our loop. Mustache has no ==, though, so the premium check became an is_premium boolean computed in code. We also tried templateFormat: "jinja2", which LangChain's Python package supports. In TypeScript it threw DEFAULT_PARSER_MAPPING[templateFormat] is not a function.

Labels and rollback. production and staging are reserved tags, and the documentation moves them in the UI. The langsmith JavaScript client has no public method that moves a tag. Our script called the same REST route the SDK uses internally (POST /api/v1/repos/-//tags). It worked, but it is not a documented API.

Caching. The SDK caches prompts for 300 seconds by default. In our test, a running app saw the new version 300 seconds after we moved the tag.

Langfuse's TypeScript client is one package, @langfuse/client. It installed 5 packages and 8 MB:

Creating a version, moving a label and reading by label are all public SDK calls: prompt.create, prompt.update and prompt.get (Get started with prompt management).

Templates. The documentation shows only {{variable}} substitution. But compile() calls the mustache library, so sections worked for our loop. The type signature accepts only string values, so passing a list needed a cast. The Langfuse UI colours the section tags red, and it lists title and body as the prompt's variables, not docs or is_premium. We would not depend on behaviour the documentation doesn't promise. When we sent the Jinja2 version instead, Langfuse returned the {% if %} and {% for %} tags unchanged, with no error. The model would have received them as text.

Caching. The cache time is 60 seconds by default (Caching). Our app saw the change after 62 seconds. Langfuse is also the only client with a fallback option: a prompt string the SDK uses when it cannot reach the server on a cold start.

Phoenix's TypeScript client fetches a prompt by name and tag, and toSDK() converts it into the message format the openai package expects. Phoenix templates only replace variables, so the condition and the loop have to run in your code before rendering:

That is 16 lines, against 6 to 8 for the other registries. All the extra lines are template logic that now lives in the app.

Templates. Phoenix offers MUSTACHE, F_STRING and NONE formats (Prompts reference). Even in MUSTACHE mode, though, rendering is a plain replacement of {{name}}. When we sent mustache sections, they came back unchanged, with no error.

Errors. getPrompt() catches every error, logs it and returns null. You can see this in the client source, src/utils/getPromptBySelector.ts. A missing prompt and an unreachable server look the same to your code, which is why the snippet checks for null.

Size and caching. The client installed 57 packages and 90 MB. Most of that is OpenTelemetry, which comes in through its @arizeai/phoenix-otel dependency. The client has no prompt cache, so every render is a network call. That is also why a label change showed up immediately: 0 seconds in our test.

AcruxCore stores Jinja2 templates and renders them on the server with nunjucks. The SDK sends the variables and gets back finished messages:

The template from the test section works as it is, condition and loop included, with no is_premium flag computed in code. A label is called an alias here, and promoteAlias() moves it (Manage prompts via the SDK). The SDK installed 3 packages and 12 MB. Most of the 12 MB is one OpenTelemetry package, @opentelemetry/semantic-conventions.

Templates. Jinja2 only. When we committed the mustache version, AcruxCore rejected it at commit time with Template parse error: unexpected token: #. That is a clear error, but it also means that moving mustache prompts from LangSmith or Langfuse requires rewriting them.

We sent the same two templates, a Jinja2 one and a mustache one, to each tool's own renderer:

The rows that matter most are the ones where the tags were left in the output, because those failures produce no error. The model receives raw template syntax, and the only symptom is a strange answer. Whatever tool you pick, test one prompt with logic in it before you move the rest.

Putting logic in the template is not automatically better. It lets someone change the condition without a deploy. It also lets them break the condition without a deploy. Keeping logic in code, as Phoenix forces you to do, puts every branch under code review and in your tests.

A registry is a new runtime dependency, so we tested an outage. The app reached each registry through a local proxy, and we switched the proxy off. A separate process then started while the registry was still unreachable.

LangSmith, Langfuse and AcruxCore keep serving the last good version while the registry is down, even after the cache time has passed. The risk is a cold start: a new container or a serverless function that boots during the outage. Langfuse's fallback option is the built-in answer to that. With the other tools, keep a copy of each prompt in your code as a fallback, which brings back part of the Git setup.

Keep prompts in Git if engineers make every prompt change and your deploys are quick. Set autoescape: false, and you get Jinja2, reviews and history for free.

Use LangSmith's prompt hub if you already use LangChain, or already trace with LangSmith. If your app doesn't use LangChain, budget for the extra dependency and for the tag moves that only the UI supports.

Use Langfuse if you want a small client, a local compile(), and a fallback for cold starts. Keep to {{variable}} substitution unless you are comfortable relying on mustache behaviour that the documentation doesn't promise.

Use Phoenix if you already use it for tracing, or if you prefer all template logic in code. Remember the null check, and that every render is a network call.

Use AcruxCore if you want real conditions and loops in the template and rendering on the server. Expect one network call per new set of variables, and a personal API key for writes.

Before you choose, run one of your own prompts with real logic in it through the tool's SDK, not through its playground. Two of the four registries we tested failed on template syntax without any error, and an SDK run is where you would see that.

#10443. The AI boom was built around Jensen Huang. What happens now?

Welcome to AI Decoded, Fast Company‘s weekly newsletter that breaks down the most important news in the world of AI. I’m Mark Sullivan, a senior writer at Fast Company, covering emerging tech, AI, and tech policy.

Sign up to receive this newsletter every week via email here. And if you have comments on this issue and/or ideas for future ones, drop me a line at sullivan@fastcompany.com, and follow me on X @thesullivan.

Jensen Huang is out, and the repercussions are just beginning

Who would have expected the AI Bubble to pop like this? Over an infidelity scandal. Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia CEO Thursday, built the company that supplied the chips that made the AI boom possible. He had the foresight to see the AI revolution coming, and formed the strategy to lock AI researchers and enterprises into his company’s CUDA software stack. 

Huang also used Nvidia’s growing chip sales windfall to prop up the growing AI industry in a dangerous way, bankrolling a webwork of AI startups, suppliers, infrastructure players, and other chip customers. Now, with a crisis of confidence in the chip company at the center, the whole AI buildout could come under considerable strain and potentially unravel. 

With all this at stake, one might wonder why Nvidia’s board and other stakeholders would want Huang to resign. But Jensen Huang’s affairs were more than marital transgressions. At least one of them had national security and geopolitical dimensions–Huang’s relationship with a Singapore-based tech executive who goes by the name Alice Huang. Not only was she a suspected Chinese spy but her company, Megaspeed, was suspected by the Commerce Department of helping funnel restricted Nvidia chips to China, the U.S.’s main rival in the AI race.  

A New York Times investigation last year found that Megaspeed’s offices in Singapore and Malaysia were largely empty, and Commerce Department officials who spoke to The Times said they found boxes of restricted Nvidia chips in a Megaspeed facility in Malaysia. It’s long been the policy of the U.S. government to reserve the fastest AI chips, most of them made by Nvidia, for U.S. and U.S.-friendly AI labs. 

Alice Huang had  Chinese “honeypot” written all over her, but Jensen Huang never caught on, or chose not to. 

The second extramarital relationship to come to light is less harmful to Nvidia but establishes a pattern of infidelity that may go further than we currently know. It involved Kimberly Powell, an Nvidia VP who led Nvidia’s health industry business. That relationship, which had for months been discussed within Nvidia, was reported this week by the New York Times after reporters spoke to Nvidia employees. Nvidia’s code of conduct warns against employees “personal relationships” that might “create conflict.” 

It all seems so sudden. After months of hand wringing about the reality of the AI boom and the stability of the enormous amounts of investment money now being plowed into building out the infrastructure needed for AI, suddenly the man at the center of it all is gone, his 33 years of leading Nvidia over. And as Creative Strategies CEO Tim Bajarin told me, there’s nobody in the world with better field vision in the AI industry than Jensen Huang.

“For much of the last decade he was the industry’s main spokesperson, explaining to customers, partners, governments and investors where computing was going and why,” says Bajarin, a long-time Silicon Valley analyst who knows Huang. “Few executives in technology have played that role . . . that is a real loss, for NVIDIA and for the ecosystem around it.”

“Still, no one is irreplaceable, and the loss of a visionary is not the same as a change in strategy,” Bajarin says. “The vision Jensen laid out is already built into NVIDIA’s roadmap, its supply chain and its people, so we do not think his departure changes where the company is going.”

Possible successors to Huang may have some pieces of the picture, but none have vision into the human relationships and deep structural dependencies that have pushed it all forward. “His right-hand man and the one who executed Jensen’s strategy is Ian Buck,” Bajarin offers. Bajarin believes Buck could be a strong candidate to succeed Huang permanently. 

Still, Huang’s affairs and subsequent resignation have already destroyed some confidence in the enormous investment being made in the AI build out. Nvidia’s stock is already off 13%. But the industry, public, and governmental reaction to Huang’s departure may be just beginning, like the first ripples of a very large stone dropped into a pond.

The real reasons Anthropic is IPO’ing first, and OpenAI later

Anthropic and OpenAI will be the first two pure-play AI companies to tap the public markets through an initial public offering. Anthropic will likely list its stock (ticker symbol: “ANT”) first, potentially on November 19, while analysts expect OpenAI, which filed its own IPO paperwork confidentially in June, to wait until early next year.

The timing of these IPOs matters a lot because both companies operate in an extremely expensive business, and they’re competing for capital from the same pool of retail and institutional investors. Both are trying to raise money at valuations well above a trillion dollars amid growing concerns about rising interest rates, volatility in technology stocks, heightened scrutiny of AI company valuations, and a decidedly negative political environment.

All about compute

Still, no artificial intelligence bubble has popped—yet—so Anthropic and OpenAI may want to go public while conditions are (relatively) good. Harrison Rolfes, an analyst at PitchBook, says it may also be a question of necessity. Both companies remain focused on buying, leasing, or building as much computing capacity as they can, even decades into the future. For a long time, they’ve relied on venture capital money and debt to cover those costs, but as private capital becomes harder to come by, they need to tap the public markets.

That may be a more urgent issue for Anthropic than for OpenAI. “The compute bills come due in December,” Rolfes tells Fast Company. Anthropic has shown impressive revenue growth during 2026, putting some real numbers behind the $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion valuation the company has proposed. “By being at this current valuation at this current time they can retain the interest and then run the momentum into the IPO,” Rolfes says.

OpenAI likely bought itself some time with the sizable capital it raised in the private markets this year, Rolfes believes. In March, the company raised $122 billion, and a recent Reuters report says OpenAI is trying to raise additional capital at a valuation of more than $1.4 trillion, locking down commitments before the Anthropic IPO. OpenAI also has a broader range of revenue sources than Anthropic, including consumer subscriptions, a growing advertising business, and licensing agreements with partners like Microsoft. OpenAI’s revenue reportedly grew more than 50% to over $10 billion in the third quarter.

A straight story

OpenAI will have to tell a clear and compelling story when it goes public—one that can withstand the scrutiny of the public markets. In fact, earlier this year, OpenAI’s CFO, Sara Friar, reportedly cited the lack of such a story as one reason her company wouldn’t be ready for a 2026 IPO.

“OpenAI’s timeline is different, and that makes sense given the company it’s building,” Jyoti Bansal, AI investor and founder of the software delivery platform Harness, tells Fast Company. “It has a different structure and a much broader business to run, spanning consumer, enterprise, infrastructure, and hardware.” OpenAI will have to clarify whether it’s primarily a consumer AI or an enterprise AI company, or how focusing equally on both could enhance and not limit overall growth in the future.

Anthropic, on the other hand, may have a slightly easier story to tell. “The business leans toward enterprise, and enterprise revenue is the kind public investors tend to value: recurring, tied to usage, and connected to real workflows,” Bansal says. “When customers are running your models in production, for coding, support and internal agents, you have a story that holds up under public-market scrutiny.”

First-mover advantage

Anthropic could see real benefits from going public first. It could set the terms by which public investors evaluate frontier AI company stocks, establishing a pricing benchmark and common metrics for measuring short- and long-term success.

This could put OpenAI in an uncomfortable position. “The $1.25 trillion that they are asking for will be compared to whatever Anthropic trades at,” Rolfes says. “So that’s the issue that OpenAI is going to face because now you have a comparable and if they can’t match that then it’s only going to cause them to get a larger discount on their value.” If OpenAI wants to command a higher valuation than Anthropic and raise more money, it will have to clearly explain to investors why it should be valued or measured differently.

OpenAI, remember, was seen as “the leading AI company” for years after the arrival of ChatGPT in late 2022. Much of that first-mover mojo is gone, but not all—it matters that millions of consumers had their first experience with AI through ChatGPT. Still, OpenAI could lose a little more mojo if it has to follow Anthropic to market.

“It puts them at a disadvantage in terms of listing first and capturing the mind share of people,” Rolfes says. “They used to be the go-to, but now if the name switches from OpenAI over to Anthropic, then it’s like, OK, maybe [Anthropic] will start to creep into the consumer mind share.”

The timing of an IPO doesn’t decide a company’s fate. In the long run, investors care more about quarter-to-quarter profitability and predictability. But pure-play AI companies are something new, and the timing of their IPOs may matter more. They have to spend unheard-of amounts of capital, some of it raised from the public markets, on infrastructure to stay competitive in the breakneck race to build state-of-the-art models. Any hiccup in plans to raise enough money for compute could leave an AI company behind in a race where catching up is exceedingly difficult. Meanwhile, its revenue opportunities—and potential shareholder returns—could shrink.

Anthropic’s new model built an operating system from an empty folder

In other Anthropic news, on Monday the AI giant released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, the same underlying model with different safeguards. In prerelease testing, the company says, an engineer asked Fable 5.2 to build a prototype operating system from an empty folder; it coordinated more than 1,000 subagents for eight days and produced one that boots on a laptop, with drivers, file storage, windows, a login screen, and an installer. Given a one-paragraph prompt, it also designed three working electronic devices—a voice-assistant hub, a USB speakerphone, and a handheld virtual pet—with circuit boards ready to manufacture in under a day. 

Netflix is calling its recommendations AI

Netflix began rolling out AI Discover, its first consumer feature branded as AI-powered, to a limited number of U.S. subscribers on supported smart TVs, Variety reported. Subscribers can choose from preset themes such as “Something Light,” “Scare Me,” and “Family Movie Night.” A “Tune Your Recommendations” button lets viewers keep a suggestion or block it from appearing again. The content is not available on kids’ profiles. Netflix has used machine learning to recommend content for years; now it’s using it to generate content.

OpenAI’s quarterly revenue crossed $10 billion

OpenAI’s quarterly revenue topped $10 billion for the first time, Bloomberg reported, a jump of roughly 50% from $6.7 billion in the second quarter, and the company’s adjusted operating margin narrowed from negative 150% to negative 109%. OpenAI’s annual revenue run rate now stands at $50 billion. Anthropic reported third-quarter revenue of $17 billion and said this week its run rate had reached $81 billion as of the end of October. (Note: the two companies calculate revenues differently: Anthropic counts the total spend on Claude models through cloud partner distributors, while OpenAI reports only its piece of the revenue-share).

Google Drive will soon prompt users to switch to Adobe Acrobat while viewing PDFs, and Gemini will get a few new tricks powered by the company’s creative suite.

The pipeline from PDFs opened in Google Drive and Gmail to Adobe Acrobat is notoriously strained. That goes for any PDF viewer, but as soon as certain tools are necessary, a large number of users rely on Adobe’s products to edit and store documents.

Google announced plans to ease the process. According to a press release today, Google will be adding a “direct pathway” from Google Drive and Gmail in Adobe Acrobat. Further detail isn’t clear, but that includes Gemini, Gemini Enterprise, and Google AI Mode in Search. It sounds like the integration will allow users to edit or manage PDFs and other files straight from Google’s AI interfaces.

It’s not just PDFs and Google Drive; Adobe’s Photoshop gets a shout, too. Expected sometimes in the future, we may see more powerful image editing powered by Gemini within Adobe Photoshop, as opposed to the current models and limitations within. Gemini Nano Banana models are currently in use, but AI generation and editing could go further with a more focused effort. Google says the push “could enable near-real-time edits,” but there’s no concrete timeline set for when we could see that.

That goes for each of these byproducts of the new partnership. Google Drive and Gmail integration with Adobe Acrobat will likely be the first to roll out, with Gemini features to follow shortly after.

SpaceX/xAI is developing a custom version of Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale AI system that replaces conventional NVLink cable assemblies with a massive 84-layer printed circuit board (PCB), in part for use in orbital data centers, reports SemiAnalysis. The system is codenamed Kessel and retains 36 Vera CPUs, 72 Rubin GPUs, and nine NVLink switch trays, but introduces a different solid-state interconnect architecture. While SpaceX/xAI will continue to buy Nvidia hardware directly from the company, Elon Musk's company will source other components independently, which could give it greater control over its hardware supply chain.

The Kessel system retains the fundamental configuration of Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 platform, which comprises 72 GPU packages distributed across 18 compute trays and nine NVLink switch trays. However, instead of Nvidia's conventional arrangement with internal NVLink cable cartridges, SpaceX plans to position compute and switch trays back-to-back around a passive PCB midplane. The architecture resembles a smaller version of Nvidia's Kyber design with 576 AI GPUs (albeit in 144 packages), which also relies on a PCB-based interconnect rather than conventional cable assemblies, SemiAnalysis notes. Interestingly, the design is aimed at both terrestrial and orbital deployments, according to the analysts.

Arguably the most distinctive feature of Kessel is its 84-layer PCB midplane, which uses ultra-low-loss M10 copper-clad laminates (CCLs). By contrast, Nvidia's Kyber architecture relied on a backplane based on a considerably more complex 156-layer PCB featuring M9 CCLs. The reduction in layer count by nearly half could substantially improve manufacturability and production yields, but the more advanced copper-clad laminate will almost certainly increase material costs. In any case, an 84-layer PCB is a device that is exceptionally hard to build.

The move to a PCB midplane could simplify system assembly by eliminating numerous high-speed cable connections, but it would not necessarily reduce manufacturing costs. An 84-layer PCB that relies on ultra-low-loss M10 laminate is an exceptionally expensive component that requires sophisticated manufacturing processes and precise quality control. To put an 84-layer PCB number into context, modern high-end server motherboards use 15 – 20 layers, whereas server development boards use more than 20 layers to virtually eliminate any electrical issues with the board itself. Furthermore, manufacturing yields of an 84-layer PCB could become a major obstacle, as defects in internal layers may render an entire board unusable. Consequently, the economic viability of Kessel will depend on whether savings from cable elimination and independent component procurement can offset the cost of its complex midplane.

Perhaps more importantly, Kessel represents a departure from Nvidia's conventional system-level procurement model. Instead of purchasing Nvidia's assembled L6 compute boards or even L10 trays that Nvidia plans to sell with its Vera Rubin generation, SpaceX reportedly plans to acquire AI accelerators, CPUs, switches, and networking components directly from Nvidia and procure other components from third-party suppliers (one can wonder how easy it will be for SpaceX/xAI to procure memory amid today's shortages). This would enable SpaceX to select its own PCB manufacturers, component vendors, and manufacturing partners, optimize its hardware for its infrastructure (which will be important for orbital deployments), and perhaps reduce intermediary costs. Meanwhile, the company would assume greater responsibility for system design, validation, manufacturing quality, and supply-chain management, which is something that most hyperscalers have been doing in recent years.

For Nvidia, the implications are less straightforward. Although direct sales of CPU and AI GPU packages could reduce the company's revenue from complete compute-board assemblies, the arrangement could also encourage other large customers to develop their own Nvidia-based systems and eventually deploy more Nvidia-based machines, something that may be important in a world where custom silicon developed by hyperscalers is rapidly gaining traction. However, to make this happen, Kessel must be a smashing success that will offer clear advantages over systems designed by Nvidia.

#10439. Burnout is a workplace safety hazard. It’s time to start treating it like one

Burnout is a huge workplace issue: the low engagement that comes with it costs every business affected a fortune. Worse yet, its effects on workers are deleterious to the point where it can literally lead to death.

Yet in my experience, most leaders consider “burnout” an HR line item to be managed by a wellness program. It’s hard to know how to jolt people out of this mindset, but if I were a CEO (and I am), I’d be very concerned about potential industrial manslaughter charges coming my way at worst, and shareholders rightfully wondering why I am failing to manage the main thing that’s materially impairing productivity at best.

Burnout is a workplace safety hazard—and needs to be governed as one. 

The World Health Organization defines burnout as the result of “chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed.” It’s a costly hazard that claims at least twice as many lives as workplace accidents. Long working hours alone led to an estimated 750,000 deaths from stroke and heart disease in 2016, more than twice the 360,000 people killed by workplace injuries, according to a report from WHO and the International Labour Organization. In the USA, workplace stressors are estimated to kill 120,000 people a year. 

Outside of the devastating human impact, the toll burnout takes on commercial performance should be triggering emergency board meetings all over the world. At an estimated cost of US $5 million a year for a company of 1,000 employees, it would be reasonable to ask very direct questions of the executive about their plans to arrest the poorly designed workplace practices that lead to burnout. 

Maybe the questions could start with who decided that it was okay to spend more than half of your working week in meetings or managing the almost 600 emails and more than 750 Teams messages knowledge workers field every week. Perhaps some questions about what the executive has done to deliberately design the working week toward outcomes—not admin. 

Burnout and chronic workplace stress come from the health of a company’s culture, and culture is almost universally dismissed, neglected or delegated to HR: A function with no formal training in organizational culture, no resources to shape it, and by its very station, no authority over the leadership behavior that does.

So, when an organization is faced with a growing number of employees taking chronic work stress-related leave—in Australia, the median time off for a serious mental health claim is almost five times that of other serious workplace injuries—it looks for a button to press, inside a function it believes has the answer. But doesn’t. 

HR has never had the answer and never will. The organizations that shape their culture with intention, and deliberately look at the accidental practices we’ve inherited from antique cultures, don’t start with HR. They look directly at:

  • the board, which needs to be asking the right questions, in line with increasing regulation and on behalf of shareholders looking for optimal productivity
  • the CEO, who is entirely accountable for the productivity and performance of the organization
  • the leaders who shape culture through the expectations they set, the practices they perpetuate, the consequences they apply for culture drift, and the chronic workplace issues they walk past every single day

CEOs and organizations never set out to burn their people out. It’s more a matter of ‘out of sight, out of mind’ and neglect. Neglecting the implications of workplace practices, neglecting better ways of working that are confirmed by research rather than the assumptions of a post-industrial era, and neglecting to look through the human lens at a growing contributor to cardiovascular incidents and death by suicide.

Whether leaders look at burnout through a productivity lens or from a human suffering perspective, the situation is clear. Leaders are enabling the ongoing, systemic impairment of commercial performance at the cost of human lives…and feeling OK about it because they’ve passed a memo to HR to invest in a wellness program or resilience training.

Thankfully, regulators and standard setters understand the crisis better and have begun something of a reckoning. ISO 45003 became the first international standard for managing psychological health and safety at work in 2021, and the US Surgeon General’s Framework for Workplace Mental Health and Well-Being names protection from harm, psychological safety included, as its first essential.

Australia has moved from guidance to enforcement. Every Australian state and territory now requires employers to identify and manage psychosocial hazards in the same way as physical ones, and in December 2025, Australia’s Department of Defence became the first federal employer convicted for failing to manage psychosocial risk.

Burnout is, quite literally, an existential risk. It’s time organizations truly started acting like it.

If this article raises concerns for you or someone you know, support is available. In the USA, call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline on 988. In Australia, call Lifeline on 13 11 14.

#10438. Can we please stop calling it a ‘honey trap’?

When Jensen Huang told Nvidia employees on November 8 that he had been “unfaithful” to his wife, there’s a phrase that quickly became omnipresent in the media: Huang had been the victim of a “honey trap,” laid by Alice Huang (no relation), a Singapore-based tech executive identified as a Chinese spy by U.S. intelligence agencies.

“Honey trap,” seriously?

The story behind the phrase is that a good, hardworking man was minding his own business when a serpent of a woman lured him off the righteous path by dishonest means and propositions he, being a man, simply couldn’t refuse. It is assumed that male sex drive is some kind of force of nature that no adult can reasonably be expected to control.

So there’s a double sexist stereotype here. Can a 63-year-old billionaire CEO really be supposed to have no say over his sex life? Like a bear wouldn’t be able to resist honey?

Anyone who, like me, grew up in the 1980s knows a close relative of this idea: the “homewrecker,” a word aimed at the other woman and never at the husband who cheated. One of the decade’s most successful films, Fatal Attraction (1987), tells the story of a married man (Michael Douglas) whose affair turns into a nightmare when the woman (Glenn Close) refuses to stay discreet and starts asking for more. The film portrays the mistress as mentally unstable and dangerous. The film ends with the wife killing the mistress and family values restored. The husband’s betrayal is never really an issue. I’m ashamed to admit that when I first watched it, some time in the 1990s, I sided completely with the poor husband, hounded by a woman the film had led me to see as a witch.

Both ideas have their roots in Genesis, where Adam, asked why he ate the forbidden fruit, answers that the woman gave it to him. It is easy scapegoating: Powerful men keep their reputation for rationality while some snake of a woman takes the blame for their lapses of judgment.

There’s a paradox that I find difficult to swallow. For centuries, women were judged too foolish to vote or hold office, yet the same culture credits them with enough cunning to bring down kings and CEOs. Men, meanwhile, are supposed to be fit to lead nations and markets while being too weak to resist the first temptation that comes their way.

Deadly clichés

The term comes from spy fiction: dictionaries credit John le Carré with popularizing “honey trap” in Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy in 1974. Espionage has long been a man’s world, and in its novels a female spy is very often a seductress. Real Cold War espionage looked quite different, since East Germany’s best-known seduction program used men, so-called Romeo agents sent west to seduce secretaries with access to government files. 

In the Nvidia story, much of the coverage of Alice Huang also draws on images Western culture has attached to Asian women for more than a century: the mysterious seductress, the Dragon Lady. In the U.S., they go back at least to the Page Act of 1875, the country’s first restrictive federal immigration law, which was enforced on the presumption that Chinese women were prostitutes. Any woman arriving from Asia had to prove she wasn’t one.

In March 2021, a white man killed eight people at three Atlanta-area spas, six of them Asian women, and police relayed his description of his victims as “sources of temptation.” Asian women end up being blamed for men’s desire. And Atlanta showed that this cliché can be deadly. Coverage casting Alice Huang as a seductress is anything but harmless.

Nobody trapped the CEO

A CEO’s sexual relationship with someone working for one of his company’s biggest customers is a clear conflict of interest. Alice Huang’s employer, Megaspeed, is said to have bought about $4.8 billion of Nvidia hardware over the past two years. In most companies, a sales manager sleeping with a key client’s buyer would be expected to disclose it and hand the account to a colleague. Nobody would describe that sales manager as “trapped,” and the CEO of one of the world’s most valuable companies, who has far more power, deserves no more indulgence.

The phrase also shrinks Alice Huang: If she is only “honey,” she cannot be much of a professional. Yet she ran a business that bought chips at enormous scale, and if the allegations hold, she will have to answer for export violations and espionage, serious crimes committed with the very agency the word denies her.

Call it what it is

The honey trap trope has consequences in the workplace. In 2019, a LeanIn.Org and SurveyMonkey survey found that 60% of male managers in the U.S. were uncomfortable mentoring, working one-on-one with, or socializing with a woman, and 36% of men said they had avoided doing so for fear of how it would look. A woman alone with a powerful man is seen as a danger to him, even though she is far more likely to be the one harassed. She also pays in lost dinners, business trips and sponsorship, the informal moments that decide who gets promoted.

Other words would be more honest. A CEO had an affair with an executive at one of his largest customers, a woman U.S. officials reportedly believe was working for Chinese intelligence, and his board is now examining whether the relationship compromised the company. It is less catchy than “honey trap,” but it treats both people as adults responsible for their choices. Isn’t that the standard any employee would expect?

#10436. Gemini 4 Carbon rolling out to Gemini app for AI Ultra, Argon remains

Following the preview at the end of last month, Google is now bringing its latest Gemini 4 Carbon model to the Gemini app.

Officially, Google says “Argon remains the ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work, while Carbon is built for tasks that test the limits of a model’s intelligence.” Examples include “complex, multi-step coding and debugging and open-ended scientific research and discovery.”

In the model picker, 4 Argon is for “Code & analysis” and 4 Carbon is for “Most complex work.” Notably, the Gemini app has removed 3.1 Pro with this launch.

To showcase performance on larger, more complex projects, Google Antigravity is previewing /swarm. This turns a “single prompt into a coordinated team of agents you can track in real time.”

Developers can assign Carbon to roles that demand the deepest reasoning, like architectural design, coordination, and auditing, while pairing it with faster, lighter models across parallel isolated workspaces and adversarial verifiers that test every change.

For legal, finance, and enterprise work, Carbon is said to bring “higher-precision knowledge work, artifact generation, and data analysis.” This includes how the model will follow “strict schemas and formatting to generate polished and precise spreadsheets, presentations, and reports.”

Existing benchmarks don’t adequately capture how agents reason natively over dense files with charts, images, blueprints, schematics, and tables, so we partnered with Artificial Analysis to launch the new Multimodal Knowledge Agents (MKA) benchmark. Carbon ranks #1 while using 3X fewer tokens than the next best model across 200 tasks that test a model’s multimodal performance in agentic workflows.

The introductory pricing for Carbon is $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens until November 30. Afterward, it will cost $4 per 1M input tokens and $20 per 1M output tokens.
