#10409. CEOs still think they can get away with affairs after #MeToo

Nearly a decade after the #MeToo movement burst into public consciousness, the upheaval at Nvidia may be a lesson in how little CEOs seem to have learned. 

Nvidia’s embattled CEO, Jensen Huang, has resigned following a New York Times report on Wednesday that revealed he had engaged in another extramarital relationship—this time involving a subordinate, the company’s vice president of healthcare and one of his 60 direct reports. The affair was a blatant violation of Nvidia’s code of conduct, which notes that employees should steer clear of situations that could create a conflict of interest, including “personal relationships.” The company also purports to “promptly investigate” reports of misconduct.

While this dalliance has fewer national security implications than his entanglement with an alleged Chinese spy, it does suggest that CEOs like Huang don’t expect to face consequences for getting involved with employees. 

Huang is in good company: Many employers have similar policies that forbid romantic relationships between managers and their direct reports, but that hasn’t stopped executives from crossing the line anyway. (Who could forget the viral video of the Astronomer CEO caught canoodling with his chief people officer at a Coldplay concert?)

In recent years, however, a number of executives have been forced to step down after pursuing inappropriate relationships, in addition to CEOs like Leslie Moonves (formerly head of CBS) being fired for sexual harassment. 

Back in 2019, McDonald’s then-CEO Steve Easterbrook was ousted over a relationship with a subordinate. Later he was sued by the company for concealing other relationships with employees and misleading investors. (He was eventually forced to pay back his $105 million severance package.)

There was Alan Shaw, former CEO of Norfolk Southern railroad, who was let go in 2024 over his relationship with the company’s chief legal officer. Last year, Nestlé SA CEO Laurent Freixe was given the boot after an internal investigation confirmed a relationship with a subordinate (which Freixe had initially denied). Kohl’s CEO Ashley Buchanan was also recently forced out when the board learned that he had given millions of dollars in business to a vendor he was dating without disclosing the relationship.

The fact that CEOs continue to pursue their subordinates, regardless of the consequences, may seem like a sign that the #MeToo movement is in the rearview. Perhaps some executives truly believe they are irreplaceable, or that there is now limited public pressure, years after #MeToo took hold. 

But Amy Nicole Baker, a professor at the University of New Haven who studies workplace romance, argues that not much has shifted after #MeToo, either in terms of CEO behavior or how companies tend to handle these situations. 

“The stock price goes down, at least in the short term,” she says, citing her research on how stock prices are impacted by sexual harassment allegations or affairs involving the CEO. “And usually CEOs are removed and replaced.”

Boards tend to have limited tolerance for the behavior, which they view as a sign of poor judgment. Indiscretions like an extramarital affair or otherwise inappropriate relationship can set off alarm bells or lead board members to wonder what else a CEO is hiding. “Boards look at CEO behavior as a signal for what could be going on in the internal management of the company,” Baker says.  

Still, it appears CEOs don’t necessarily feel constrained by those expectations, or the rules they impose on their employees—even when their own peers have been in the line of fire. 

“People show less restraint when they are in power, and they’re also more likely to perceive someone else sending them sexual signals when they’re actually not,” Baker says. “So the research on power can tell us a little bit about why this keeps happening.” 

People in positions of power tend to be more impulsive and comfortable with risk—something they are often rewarded for in a business context. Company culture can also reinforce that behavior, if it’s more informal and encourages people to push boundaries. “If you’re willing to break a rule in one way, it’s probably more acceptable to tacitly break a rule in a different way,” Baker says. 

The intense scrutiny of Huang’s misdeeds might discourage some CEOs from engaging in relationships with subordinates or other inappropriate behavior—but likely not for long. 

“In terms of the CEOs and their propensity to get involved in risky workplace relationships, that doesn’t seem to have changed,” Baker says. “More people are willing to say, ‘Yes, this happened to me. Yes, this is an issue. Yes, this is a problem.’ There’s certainly more recognition and awareness. But when it comes to people at this highest echelon, I’m not seeing a change in behavior.”

Venice-X maxes out the family's frequency for the first time.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

AMD missed out on deploying Turin-X CPUs in the previous generation, giving its 3D V-Cache tech a four-year hiatus from the data center following the launch of Genoa-X in 2023. In the second half of next year, 3D V-Cache is coming back for HPC with Venice-X, matching the 96 cores and 1,152 MB of L3 cache available on the EPYC 9684X (Genoa-X), but with vastly higher clock speeds, PCIe 6.0, and nearly four times the per-socket memory bandwidth.

After first bringing hybrid bonding to EPYC processors with Milan-X in 2022, AMD followed up a little over a year later with Genoa-X. Turin came and went without a chip sporting stacked SRAM, but now, it’s back with Venice-X. The critical change this time around doesn’t come from big jumps in core count — and consequently cache — as is the case with the standard SP7 lineup. Rather, it’s the 5.3 GHz boost clock speed, another pillar of Venice broadly, that’s particularly beneficial in the HPC workloads Venice-X targets.

As you can see from the top EPYC -X chips from previous generations, boost clocks were significantly lower for the X chips, and higher frequencies were available within the standard chips from each family. Milan scaled up to 4.1 GHz, while Genoa could climb to 4.4 GHz, just not on the EPYC -X chips. Venice-X brings up to the maximum 5.3 GHz boost clock available across the range, unifying a high frequency with a large pool of bonded L3 for HPC workloads.

There are still details missing about Venice-X, including the base frequency, how many SKUs are in the lineup and what their specs are, and the TDP (though the 400 to 600 W range available to other Venice CPUs is likely). The chips appear to use the SP7 socket, however, keeping with previous EPYC -X chips.

The platform comes with 96 PCIe 6.0 lanes, while the smaller SP8 platform targeting enterprises trades memory channels for PCIe lanes. Venice-X comes with the full 16-channel memory setup available on SP7, including support for MRDIMMs at 12,800 MT/s that can drive the quoted 1.6 TB/s of per-socket memory bandwidth.

The critical marriage with Venice-X for HPC workloads, according to AMD, is high frequency with a large pool of stacked cache. AMD currently maintains both 3D V-Cache and high-frequency EPYC chips in its HPC fleet to run its internal EDA workloads. AMD Fellow Phil Steinke says the company runs performance analysis on these workloads to characterize performance, optimize EPYC designs, and push partners to optimize their software.

The biggest consumer on the HPC fleet by far are function verification workloads at over half of AMD's used compute, according to Steinke. These are logic simulations that show up in tools like Cadence Xcelium, and Steinke says the EPYC team is running these workloads “24 x 7 x 365.”

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

An example of one such workload is above, measuring IPC with AMD's uProf monitoring utility. With 3D V-Cache, AMD says this workload completes 40% faster at around double the instructions per clock. AMD didn't clarify which chips it was comparing or what application it was using. However, the comparison is between an EPYC fleet with and without 3D V-Cache.

Steinke says AMD is able to now move toward a single chip with Venice-X, maintaining the cache advantages in workloads like functional verification while driving the EDA workloads more sensitive to frequency. "I mentioned we have a mix of high frequency and 3D V-Cache CPUs in our data center, and that's because through Milan and Genoa, the high frequency parts were always a little higher on the frequency side," Steinke said. "You don't have that dichotomy [with Venice-X]. You can get the best of both worlds in a single CPU, and this is what we're really excited to be picking up for our own use."

AMD hasn't shared any benchmarks for Venice-X yet, but it provided some more specific HPC benchmarks comparing its high-frequency EPYC 9686F to Intel's Xeon 6980P in several HPC workloads, such as computational fluid dynamics. In AMD's testing, the 9686F was 1.6x faster in these benchmarks while running 32 fewer cores.

We had a chance to test the EPYC 9686F along with the dense EPYC 9996, which you can read more about in our Zen 6 EPYC Venice deep dive and benchmarking article. And indeed, the EPYC 9686F looks very impressive in some of the HPC workloads we ran.

We were only able to test a 2P configuration, and as evidenced by the sole Xeon 6980P, CloverLeaf is sensitive to latency. Even then, the 2P EPYC 9686F completed the complex hydrodynamics simulation in about a third of the time as a single Xeon 6980P.

AMD says it's currently using MEXT, its AI-driven flash-as-DRAM technology, to bolster the amount of memory available for its EDA workloads. When it deploys Venice-X, Steinke says the company will continue using MEXT, which you can read more about in our recent MEXT breakdown on Tom's Hardware Premium.

Venice-X CPUs are launching in the second half of 2027, while SP7 and SP8 Venice CPUs are rolling out now. Also coming in the second half of next year is AMD's Verano, which it's pitching as an AI host node that leverages SOCAMM2 LPDDR5X memory.

#10405. Kalshi will pay you $120,000 to play ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’

People are already calling out sick to play the feverishly anticipated Grand Theft Auto VI. Companies like Logitech are even giving staff paid time off to partake. 

Now, thanks to prediction market Kalshi, folks won’t have to play hooky from their jobs to dive into the video game—the first installment in 13 years of Rockstar Games’ hit franchise that has earned the company billions worldwide. Instead, one person can make playing it their literal job.

Kalshi will pay a lucky gamer between $100,000 and $120,000 to play Grand Theft Auto VI’s story mode through to completion, starting right at midnight on launch day, November 19. The winning applicant will stream their digital criminal adventures on YouTube or Twitch as they explore the fictional U.S. state of Leonida as the Bonnie-and-Clyde main character couple, Jason and Lucia.

The ideal candidate is “an experienced gamer” and “streamer with your own channel,” the listing states, along with “18+ years of life IRL, 10+ years of sweaty gaming, 3+ years of streaming experience.” They’ll get an extra $15,000 upon completion of the project.

As Kalshi’s “researcher”—and yes, per the LinkedIn post, the company assures that this is a real job—the winning candidate will be tasked with exploring and studying Leonida’s in-game economy of robberies and heists, perfecting the “optimal moneymaking strategy” and building “a spreadsheet to prove it,” to the point where they’ll get “accused of ruining the game for everyone else.”

In addition to unpacking the way fictional money moves in Vice City, the researcher is apparently also tasked with monitoring the game’s effects on the actual economy—tracking, for example, “who called in ‘sick,’ how DoorDash carried the entire nation through launch week, and how much productivity America lost,” the listing states. 

Kalshi’s interest in the cultural and economic impacts of the game are well founded: The Wall Street Journal has warned of a “work blackout” upon its release, and one Spanish economist estimated the U.S. economy will lose $1 billion in productivity due to absenteeism.

And according to a poll released last month that surveyed 1,000 U.S. adults 18 or older who are employed full time and play video games regularly, 39% said they were planning to request time off in advance to play GTA VI, 36% said they’ll call in sick, and 32% said they’d “work” from home on release day. Many anticipate catching “GTA flu.”

Grand Theft Auto VI, which is being called “the biggest entertainment launch in history,” arrives Thursday, November 19, on the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X and S consoles. Digital preorders have broken records, generating $1 billion from over 10 million units sold worldwide, according to estimates.

The researcher listing hasn’t even been up for 24 hours, and “over 100 people have clicked apply,” according to the LinkedIn post—something nobody needed Kalshi to predict.

#10404. Google Fi brings back network switching with ‘secondary’ partner, expands W+ beyond Pixel

Google Fi Wireless is rolling out a big update today with the return of network switching thanks to a “secondary” partner.

Google Fi is now bringing back a second partner as part of its new “super network.” Most users will be on the “Primary network,” but Google Fi will automatically switch users to the “Secondary network” if it meaningfully improves performance with so-called “smart thresholds” for doing so. At launch, there is no manual switching.

Google is not naming the second network today, but did share that Ultra Wideband is supported. Officially, you are switching between “two of America’s fastest 5G networks.”

Network switching will first be supported on Pixel 9 and newer devices that have a Google Fi eSIM (and no other SIM active). It makes use of Android’s Multiple Enabled Profiles (MEP) eSIM technology that allows for two carrier profiles on a single chip.

It might be important to note that T-Mobile actually bought out Sprint, and added their towers to their network so its safe to say that Google Fi still works with the same coverage as before the merger.

The Google Fi app gains a “Your super network” card in the Home tab that shows whether you’re connected to the Primary or Secondary network. “See activity” lets you view switching history and when it last occurred. Google will also note if you’re in range of W+ networks.

Google today is also expanding its Wi-Fi Auto Connect+ network beyond Pixel phones to select Samsung Galaxy (S23, Fold/Flip 5, and newer) and modern Motorola phones. These premium Wi-Fi networks are available in millions of airports, malls, stores, and restaurants. The connection happens automatically, with the Google Fi Virtual Carrier Network encrypting data.

The final update today sees the companion app gain “Ask Fi.” This AI-powered chat is meant to quickly provide answers and guided troubleshooting for common issues. You can request human support with seamless handoff that keeps the chat context.

These Google Fi updates start rolling out today, with network switching seeing gradual availability. This launch is accompanied by several deals:

#10400. From User Feedback to a Better Prompt: 4 Tools Tested in TypeScript

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

When an LLM app gives a wrong answer, nothing in your logs shows it. The request returns 200, the JSON is valid, and no exception fires. Usually the user is the only one who notices. A thumbs-down button records that moment, on the exact trace that went wrong, while the user still remembers why.

That button is easy to add. The hard part is what comes after: turning the thumbs-down into a reviewed test case, a judge score, and a better prompt.

We ran that loop in TypeScript in four tools: LangSmith, Langfuse, Phoenix and AcruxCore. All four handled the first four steps, which are user feedback, reviewer comments, a dataset and an LLM judge. Only AcruxCore rewrote the prompt from TypeScript. On 15 support tickets that no tool had seen, the rewritten prompt routed 13 correctly, against 7 for the original.

Our test app is a support-ticket router. It reads a ticket and returns JSON with a category (account, billing, bug or feature_request) and a priority (P0, P1 or P2). The first version of the prompt describes only the output format:

The support team has a policy that this prompt never states. Sign-in problems are always account. A customer who can't use the product at all is P0. Any billing error is P1, even when the customer says there is no rush. Feature requests are P2, however angry the customer sounds.

Without that policy, the model guesses priority from the customer's tone. Here are three real replies from the first version:

Every reply is valid JSON, so no schema check catches the mistake. A person has to read the reply and say it is wrong. The loop in this article takes that judgement and turns it into a better prompt.

All four tools cover evaluation. We compared the self-hosted ones on tracing in Self-Hosted LangSmith Alternatives: 4 Tools Tested on One TypeScript Agent, and on prompt registries in Prompt Management in TypeScript. For a broader comparison of self-hosted options, see this LangSmith alternatives roundup. This article covers the feedback loop only.

We wrote 30 tickets. Fifteen are the "production traffic" that each tool's app processed. The other 15 are a holdout set. No tool saw them, and we used them only for the final before-and-after check.

Each tool ran the same sequence from one TypeScript script:

The reviewer comments follow one template, so the wording is identical in every tool:

The comments name one rule each. The full policy appears nowhere in the data any tool received.

The app model isn't fully deterministic at temperature 0. Each tool's run got between 6 and 8 of the 15 traffic tickets right, so the tools received 7 to 9 thumbs-down each. The holdout check below repeats every measurement three times.

All four tools accept feedback on a trace from TypeScript. They differ in how a second person, the reviewer, adds the correct answer.

LangSmith stores both as feedback on a run. The thumbs-down runs go into an annotation queue, where a reviewer adds feedback with a comment:

Langfuse stores both as scores. An annotation queue needs a score config first:

Phoenix stores both as span annotations. The reviewer's comment goes in explanation:

Phoenix stores spans asynchronously. Our first run annotated a span before Phoenix had stored it, and the API returned a 404. The script now waits until all 15 spans are visible.

AcruxCore stores both as feedback rows on the trace. The source field separates the end user from the reviewer:

This is the first step where the code differs a lot. Each tool can make a dataset, but only one builds it from feedback in one call.

In LangSmith, a run query finds the thumbs-down runs. Then createExamples copies them into a dataset. You decide where the reviewer's comment goes. We put it in the reference output:

LangSmith can also do this without code. An automation rule in the UI can add runs that match a filter to a dataset.

In Langfuse, the scores API finds the thumbs-down traces. Two details cost us a run each. A boolean score is filtered with value: "false", not 0. And the trace ID is returned only when you ask for the subject field group:

In Phoenix, getSpans can't filter by annotation. So the script lists the app's spans, reads their annotations, and keeps the ones with a thumbs-down. Then createDataset takes the examples. We kept the source span ID in the metadata.

In AcruxCore, buildFromFeedback takes the reviewer's feedback IDs. Each comment becomes that example's grading criteria, and the input comes from the variables captured on the trace:

Each tool scored the first version of the prompt on its own dataset. The judge read the reviewer's comment and the router's reply, and returned 1 for a match and 0 for a mismatch.

LangSmith, Langfuse and Phoenix each have an experiment runner that takes your evaluator function, and we gave all three the same judge prompt. AcruxCore grades with its built-in judge inside the optimize run. All four used the same judge model.

The first version fails almost every reviewed case. That is expected, because these are the cases users marked wrong. A score of 1 means the app model got that case right on the second call, or the judge accepted a wrong reply. We didn't check which.

The judge can also run without your code. Besides the in-code evaluator we used, Langfuse has a managed LLM-as-a-judge that runs on production traces and on experiments, with your own judge prompt. LangSmith has online evaluators, which you set up in its UI, for the same job.

An optimizer reads the failing cases and the reviewer comments, writes new versions of the prompt, and scores each one with the judge. This is the step that turns feedback into a better prompt, and it's where the four tools differ most.

LangSmith's API reference lists an optimize prompt job (POST /api/v1/repos/optimize-job). It takes a prompt name, a dataset name, evaluator IDs and an algorithm, promptim or demo. No method in the TypeScript SDK wraps it, so we called it with fetch. We gave it a code evaluator that checks the reply against the reviewer's correct answer.

The job was accepted and reported successful about ten seconds later. It ran no experiment on the dataset. With auto_commit set to true, it added no new commit to the prompt. We found no guide for this endpoint, so we may have configured it wrongly, but the job record and its logs gave no error to act on.

LangSmith's documented route to prompt optimization is promptim, which its README calls an experimental library. It is a Python package with a CLI, and it can add a human review step through LangSmith annotation queues.

Langfuse has no optimizer. Its blog shows a workflow with Claude Code agent skills that reads Langfuse data and edits the prompt. That workflow runs in a coding agent, not in your app's code.

Phoenix's Optimize Prompts Automatically tutorial uses Arize's prompt-learning package, which you clone from GitHub and install with pip. The Phoenix TypeScript client has no optimizer export, and the tutorial runs outside Phoenix. Arize's commercial platform, Arize AX, has prompt optimization built in.

For Python teams, there are more options: Opik's Agent Optimizer and DSPy both rewrite prompts from a dataset and a metric. This article covers TypeScript.

Its optimize run takes the dataset and drafts three rewrites of the production prompt. It runs each rewrite and the current production version on every example, and the judge grades all of them:

The three rewrites tied, so we took candidate A. Its rationale: "Added explicit priority rules for each category and clarified that access-blocking issues are P0, billing errors are P1, and feature requests are P2, overriding tone/urgency." The Improve a prompt from feedback guide covers the dashboard version of this step.

A rewrite that passes the cases it was built from can still fail on new tickets. So we ran both prompts on the 15 holdout tickets, three times each, outside every tool. The script calls the model directly and checks the category and the priority against the expected answer. No judge is involved.

Both come from one line in the rewrite: "P1 for bugs without workaround." That rule isn't in the team's policy, and no reviewer wrote it. The optimizer made it up to explain the examples it had. There was also no outage in the traffic set's thumbs-down cases, because the first version routed that one correctly. So no comment ever said that a full outage is P0.

The optimizer learns only from what users marked wrong. Anything they never marked stays a guess, and the rationale won't tell you which rules are guesses. Read the rewritten prompt before you promote it.

In LangSmith, Langfuse and Phoenix, shipping a new version is a tag or label move. We showed those calls in the prompt-management article. Here there was no rewrite to ship, so the step didn't apply.

In AcruxCore, promotion commits the candidate as a new prompt version and moves the production alias to it. Nothing else moves:

The app renders production on every call, so the next ticket used version 2 without a deploy.

Use LangSmith if your team already works in it and writes Python. Feedback, queues, datasets and experiments all work from TypeScript, and promptim covers optimization from Python.

Use Langfuse if you want a managed judge that runs on live traces with your own prompt. Plan to write the dataset glue code and the rewrite step yourself.

Use Phoenix if you already trace with OpenTelemetry and annotate spans. Plan to move to Python, or to Arize AX, for optimization.

Use AcruxCore if you want all six steps from TypeScript in one tool, including the rewrite. Keep a human on the promote button.

#10398. Wyze’s new door lock has speedy fingerprint recognition and 12-month battery life

Wyze is today launching its new “Lever Lock,” a smart lock for your front door that has a year of battery life and fast fingerprint recognition, all for an affordable price tag.

Available starting today, the Wyze Level Lock is not your typical deadbolt smart lock. Rather, this is a smart lock designed for your standard single-bore latch, meaning it’s available for doors that other smart locks aren’t compatible with. You can still have a deadbolt, but you’ll need enough space for both (per Wyze’s guidelines below).

The Lever Lock has a PIN entry and a fingerprint sensor, the latter of which Wyze says recognizes your fingerprint in about half a second. It uses local storage for biometric data and works to improve that data with each successful unlock.

The PIN has a clever feature (though it’s presented in somewhat poor taste) that lets you input random digits before or after your actual code to prevent onlookers from being able to see your code. There’s also a physical key backup as well as a USB-C input on the outside in the case that the battery dies – Wyze says it lasts about 12 months on a charge using eight AA batteries.

The Wyze Lever Lock is available today for $99.98 and shipping immediately.

Huang was reportedly captured on video being affectionate with a direct report

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang — already embroiled in a scandal for an extramarital relationship with a woman believed by U.S. intelligence to be spying on behalf of China — reportedly had a separate affair with one of his direct reports, according to the New York Times. Nvidia's board is now reportedly preparing to fire Huang.

The Times, citing five anonymous sources within Nvidia, says that Huang had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company's vice president of health care. The sources claim that Huang and Powell were "captured on video being affectionate" in March at a hotel in San Jose, Calif., where the company's GTC conference takes place.

That report says that someone at the hotel filmed the moment on their smartphone, but that Huang's security team "sequestered" them and "made the person an offer to sign a nondisclosure agreement."

Powell joined Nvidia in 2008 and has been steadily promoted. The Times highlights that personal relationships are mentioned as potentially causing conflicts of interest in Nvidia's code of conduct. Like Huang, she is married to someone else.

In 2018, former Intel CEO Brian Krzanich resigned following a relationship with an employee, which was also against the company's policies. Nvidia has not responded to a request for comment from Tom's Hardware. This story will be updated if we hear back.Earlier this week, it came out that Jensen had an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, formerly a top executive at Singaporean firm Megaspeed and believed by U.S. intelligence to be a spy. Huang admitted to the affair in an email to Nvidia employees. China has denied claims of espionage.Nvidia's board has an ongoing investigation into that affair, led by the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz. Huang is continuing to run the company while that investigation is ongoing. Law firms have been racing to sue the company on behalf of shareholders, including a proposed class-action lawsuit that Nvidia misled investors on material facts about the business.

The Congressional House committee on China has called on Huang for a closed-door session, with Republican lawmakers saying the reports "raise significant national security concerns."

Huang has been a leader of the AI industry, providing the most sought-after chips in the field. He has also had the ear of President Donald Trump, traveling with him and attempting to influence export controls.Trump told reporters that the FBI was investigating Huang, but also that the Nvidia CEO "had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.”

Like last year, the next Pixel Drop is rolling out a month early in November. Coupled with Android 17 QPR2, it’s quite a big Feature Drop for Gemini and other AI capabilities, as well as the Pixel 10 series.

Pixel Watch Drop: Create My Widget, Phone-to-Watch Unlock, and Wear OS 7.1

Gemini Intelligence is coming to the Pixel 10, Pixel 10 Pro, Pixel 10 Pro XL, and Pixel 10 Pro Fold. The lead feature is Rambler to automatically remove filler words and format your transcription.

The Pixel 10 series also gets Gemini app automation for ordering groceries, ride-sharing, meal delivery, marketplace transactions, and booking reservations. Proactive Gemini Actions let you “send groceries right to your Google Keep list straight from ongoing conversations” and more.

The Pixel 11 and 10 are getting Create My Widget. This generative UI capability lets you create custom homescreen objects using natural language. For example, you can create a sports widget or an event countdown. The feature first debuted on Googlebooks.

On the Pixel 11, Gemini Call Screen is an “intelligent, proactive assistant that screens incoming inquiries on demand.” Replacing Manual Call Screen, Gemini will speak to callers in a more conversational manner than before.

Meanwhile, the Pixel 10+ now lets Gemini make calls on your behalf in the US. Use cases include changing reservations, putting items on hold, and checking inventory. Beta testing started in September.

The AI features continue with 10 new Custom Icon styles. Following the March introduction, Google has upgraded the experience with Nano Banana for higher-quality icons. Available on Pixel 6a+.

Pixel Solver in the Google Calculator app provides generative AI custom templates and allows for conversational, multi-step problem solving using prompts. This is available on Pixel 11+.

Unit Conversion is a “top-tier module” that saves you from switching between your browser and the Calculator app. It offers inline mathematics, combined unit interpretation, and real-time exchange rates on the Pixel 6a+.

On the Pixel 11 Pro, Pro XL, and Pro Fold, HiLight now supports Google Messages notifications after being restricted to phone calls and Gemini at launch.

Pixel Search is now available on the Pixel 6 and newer to provide a more integrated on-device lookup experience that spans apps, web, settings, and other personal content. It allows for natural language search from the search bar at the top of the app grid.

I suspect a lot of these will be server side/app updates. When I went to settings to check for the update I already noticed the new family hub so it was live even before I installed the new version.

One thing I noticed immediately on my 9 Pro is that the battery life is much better. It's been pretty abysmal lately, I thought it might battery degradation but here we are, it's much improved, fingers crossed it'll stay like that. That alone was worth the update.

Extreme Battery Charging is now available on the Pixel 10 series.

Following the 2.0 redesign in September, Pixel VIPs now supports Live Location Sharing. This will surface real-time information and battery status from Find Hub in contact cards and homescreen widgets on the Pixel 6a+.

Transit Mode has been upgraded to automatically trigger based on device sensors. This is available on the Pixel 6a+.

#10392. November Pixel Watch Drop: Create My Widget, Phone-to-Watch Unlock, and Wear OS 7.1

Besides a big update for phones, there’s also a sizable Pixel Watch Drop today, but it’s mostly a preview of what’s to come.

On the Pixel Watch 3 and newer (Wear OS 7+), step-by-step workouts are rolling out starting today. In addition to instructions, you can log reps and weights, as well as track metrics. Make sure you’re on Google Health 4.12+ on your Pixel Watch and version 5.12+ on Android.

The other four features previewed today will be available in the next few weeks.

Phone-to-Watch unlock is such a welcome addition!

As for "workouts on watch", that's something I was expecting when I first purchased the Pixel Watch 2 about 6 months ago. Since then I moved to PW3, and while I was super disappointed such a basic feature wasn't available (what's the point of all custom workouts on the phone app if they can't be run on the watch!?), I'm super glad that this feature they've announced at the release of Pixel Watch 5 is now being rolled out also to Pixel Watch 3 and 4!

With the Wear OS 7.1 update, the Pixel Watch 3 and newer will summarize “extensive” notification clusters and multi-message chats into overviews. This requires a paired Pixel 9 (excluding the A-Series) or newer.

Like on phones and Googlebooks, Create My Widget lets you create custom displays of information on the Pixel Watch 4 and newer.

Manual Call Screen is becoming Gemini Call Screen on the Pixel Watch 5. This “proactive, agentic feature” will filter incoming calls on demand and generate key details in US English.

The final feature lets your nearby phone unlock the Pixel Watch instead of having to manually enter the PIN or pattern on a small screen. After unlocking your phone, a prompt (“Unlocking your watch”) appears at the top of the screen with a button to “Cancel.” Your watch must be on your wrist to unlock. This will be available on the Pixel Watch 3 and newer, with UWB playing a role in the process.

#10390. Friendly Fraud Prevention for Developers: What to Log, Block and Automate

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Friendly fraud prevention comes down to three jobs you can do in code: log the right checkout data, block risky payments before they settle, and automate your response when a dispute still lands. Get the first one wrong and you can't win the dispute later, no matter how good your case is.

In this tutorial, we'll build each piece in Node.js in a way that works with any payment service provider (PSP). Your code owns the data and the logic, and a thin adapter talks to Stripe, Adyen, Checkout.com or whoever processes your payments.

Friendly fraud happens when a customer makes a real purchase, then disputes it with their card issuer. They might claim they didn't authorize it, that it never arrived, or that they canceled. Sometimes it's honest confusion. A spouse used the saved card, or the charge showed up under a name they didn't recognize. Sometimes it's a free refund with extra steps.

Either way, the money leaves your account. A dispute (also called a chargeback) reverses the payment, and your processor charges a dispute fee on top. Lose too many, and the card networks put your account into a monitoring program with higher fees.

It's also common. Visa puts friendly fraud at around 20% of fraudulent disputes globally, and up to 30% for high-volume online merchants. Mastercard goes further: it says first-party fraud makes up 75% of the fraud online businesses experience.

So why is this your problem and not finance's? Because the evidence that wins these disputes is created at checkout, by your code. If your app never stored the customer's IP address, device ID or login history, nobody can produce it three months later when the dispute arrives.

Friendly fraud can be stopped at four points, and each one is a different piece of code:

Most guides only cover stages 1 and 4. The rest of this tutorial walks through all four.

Log four things on every order: the customer's IP address, a device ID, their account ID and the shipping address. Those are the data elements Visa's Compelling Evidence 3.0 (CE3.0) rules check when you fight an "unauthorized" fraud dispute.

Here's how CE3.0 works. You win the dispute if you can show two earlier, undisputed purchases on the same card, made 120 to 365 days before the disputed one. All three purchases must share at least two data elements, and one of them must be the IP address or device ID. In plain terms: same card, same person, same device, and they never complained before.

Most PSPs support CE3.0, including Stripe, Adyen, Checkout.com and Airwallex. But none of them can submit data you never captured. And because the window reaches back a full year, you need to keep these logs for at least 13 months (Mastercard's rule, below).

Mastercard has its own version, called First-Party Trust, for disputes filed under reason code 4837 (no cardholder authorization). It asks for one data point from each of three categories: a device factor (IP address, device ID or fingerprint), a delivery factor (shipping address, email or phone) and a different identity factor (such as account login ID or billing address). On the dispute route, Mastercard calls a lookup service that you host, with named fields such as deviceIpAddress, orderDeviceId, orderEmail and userIdName. That service has to answer in about 2.5 seconds on average and search 13 months of sales data.

First-Party Trust is live in the US. Per Mastercard's October 2026 announcement, it reaches Eastern Europe, the Middle East and Africa from October 2026 and the rest of Europe from July 2027. If you sell into Europe, the logging work is due now.

The good news: one evidence table serves both networks. Capture the data once, then keep the eligibility checks for Visa and Mastercard separate.

Start with a table that stores this data per order, separate from your PSP:

Then capture it in your checkout route. If your app sits behind a proxy or CDN, set Express's trust proxy so req.ip returns the customer's address, not your load balancer's:

The psp object is your adapter: one small module per provider that maps its API to the same shape. Swap providers, and this route doesn't change.

For digital products and SaaS, log usage too. Login timestamps, downloads and feature activity prove the customer used what they paid for, which beats "I never received it" claims.

The cheapest dispute is the one that never happens. Three checkout changes do most of the work: 3D Secure on risky payments, a billing descriptor customers recognize, and a few rules that stop obvious abuse.

Use 3D Secure where risk is higher. 3D Secure (3DS) asks the cardholder to confirm the payment with their bank, often through an app prompt. For authenticated payments, liability for fraud disputes generally shifts from you to the card issuer. Every major PSP supports it, and most let you request it per payment instead of forcing it on everyone. Forcing it everywhere adds friction and costs conversions, so trigger it on risk signals.

Make your billing descriptor obvious. The descriptor is the text on the customer's card statement. If it reads PMT*SRV 8812 instead of your product name, expect "I don't recognize this charge" disputes. Use the brand name customers know, and add a support URL or phone number where your PSP allows it. If you sell several products, use a dynamic descriptor that names each one.

Add a risk check before you charge. Most PSPs include a rules engine, but a small check in your own code keeps the logic portable:

Store the signals array with the order. If a dispute arrives later, you'll know whether the payment looked risky at the time, which helps you decide whether to fight it or accept it.

Keep the rules few and specific. A rule that blocks 5% of good customers to stop 1% of bad ones costs more than the disputes it prevents.

Yes, if you ship physical goods. The window between a successful payment and the moment an order ships is the cheapest place to stop friendly fraud: nothing has left the warehouse, so canceling costs you nothing but the sale. Most fraud tools decide at checkout and never look again.

The pattern is a fulfillment gate. Instead of sending every paid order straight to your warehouse or 3PL, route it through a decision step first:

The verify path does two jobs. Legitimate buyers confirm and their order ships. Buyers planning to dispute see that the store is watching, and a confirmed verification becomes evidence if they dispute anyway.

The hard part is screenOrder. Your own data only shows how a customer behaved with you. A buyer who has filed "item not received" disputes at 10 other stores looks brand new on their first order with yours. That's why post-purchase screening works best on shared data across many merchants.

Chargeflow Prevent is one example of this kind of friendly fraud prevention. It scores each order after checkout and before fulfillment, links device, IP, email and payment behavior across a network of 20,000+ merchants, and returns approve, verify or cancel. Today it runs as a Shopify app, with no checkout changes. A public Prevent API isn't available yet, so on other stacks you'd build the gate above with your own rules and data.

Build an order lookup endpoint. When a cardholder taps "I don't recognize this" in their banking app, the issuer can now ask the merchant for order details before a dispute is filed. Visa does this through Verifi Order Insight, and Mastercard through Ethoca Consumer Clarity. Show the customer a receipt with your logo, the items and the delivery date, and many disputes are never filed.

One endpoint can serve both networks, plus Mastercard's First-Party Trust dispute route. Mastercard's published service levels for this kind of lookup are strict:

The tricky part is matching. Issuers often send partial data, so match on whatever arrives: acquirer reference number (ARN), authorization code, date, amount, currency, and card BIN plus last four digits.

On top of lookups, Visa and many PSPs offer rules-based auto-refunds. Verifi's Rapid Dispute Resolution (RDR) and Visa Resolve refund pre-disputes that match rules you set, such as "refund anything under $25". You don't write code for these, but you do pick the thresholds, so treat them like the REFUND_THRESHOLD below.

If you sell subscriptions, many friendly fraud disputes aren't about stolen cards at all. The customer forgot about a renewal, couldn't find the cancel button, or thinks they canceled. Each of these has a code fix.

Here's a daily job that sends renewal reminders and records that each one went out:

That evidenceLog row matters. When a customer later claims they never knew about the renewal, you can show the exact date you told them.

Automate two things: refunding payments that get flagged before they become chargebacks, and building evidence packets for the ones you fight. Both run off webhooks, and both have hard deadlines that humans miss.

Card networks can warn you before a dispute is filed. Visa runs this through Verifi and Mastercard through Ethoca, and many PSPs pass these alerts or their own early fraud warnings to you by webhook. Refunding at this stage costs you the sale, but you skip the dispute fee and the dispute doesn't count against your ratio.

The threshold is a business call. Refunding a $20 order is cheaper than fighting it; a $900 order with strong evidence may be worth contesting.

When a fraud dispute arrives, check whether it qualifies for CE3.0 by looking for two earlier undisputed orders on the same card that share data with the disputed one:

If you get two matches, pass them to your PSP's CE3.0 evidence fields. On Stripe that's evidence.enhanced_evidence.visa_compelling_evidence_3; other PSPs have their own equivalents. Your adapter handles the mapping. If not, fall back to standard evidence: the IP, receipt, usage logs, renewal reminders and terms acceptance you've been logging all along.

Always submit before the deadline your PSP returns with the dispute. A late response is an automatic loss.

The code above covers the basics. A production system also needs evidence templates per reason code, network deadlines per card brand, retries, and win-rate tracking. That maintenance multiplies with every PSP you add.

PSP-native tools only see that PSP's data, so they miss the usage logs, renewal reminders and support threads in your own app. A dedicated platform connects to your PSPs and lets you send that data in.

Here's what the buy path looks like with the Chargeflow API. Chargeflow ingests disputes from connected PSPs (Stripe, PayPal, Adyen, Checkout.com, Braintree and 20+ others), fires a dispute.created webhook, and you enrich the dispute with the evidence you logged:

Chargeflow then builds the response and submits it to the PSP before the deadline. Pre-dispute alerts work the same way: Chargeflow can refund flagged transactions for you, or send alerts.created and alerts.transaction.linked webhooks so your code issues the refund and reports the result to POST /alerts/{id}/outcome.

Using Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor to build this? Chargeflow publishes its whole developer documentation as one machine-readable file, docs.chargeflow.io/llms-full.txt. Point your assistant at it and it can write the webhook handler and field mapping against the real API, not a guess.

Then your merchants get the disputes, and you need to give them a dispute product without building a dispute team. Chargeflow Connect is built for this. It exposes the same prevention, alerts and recovery engine to your platform in a few delivery models:

EaaS is the most developer-friendly entry point. You POST /public/2025-04-01/evidence with a merchant account_id and a dispute, get back an in_progress record, and receive an evidence.ready webhook with the PDF link, typically in about 30 seconds. Store the evidence id, not the URL, because the download link expires after 7 days. You can run it on auto-pilot (Chargeflow generates and submits) or co-pilot (your merchant approves first).

Don't wait for a customer to dispute a charge to find out your evidence pipeline is broken. Most PSPs give you test cards that create disputes on demand.

One more check before launch: confirm your webhook endpoints verify signatures and return 200 fast. PSPs and Chargeflow retry deliveries that fail, and a slow handler can process the same dispute twice.

If you only do one thing this week, start logging IP address and device ID on every order. Everything else builds on that data.

True fraud is when a criminal uses a stolen card. Friendly fraud is when the real cardholder makes a purchase, then disputes it. Prevention differs: true fraud is stopped at checkout with risk checks and 3DS, while friendly fraud is won with evidence after the fact.

Mostly, yes. Both describe a real cardholder disputing a legitimate charge. "Chargeback fraud" usually implies the customer did it on purpose, while friendly fraud also covers honest mistakes, like a forgotten subscription or a family member's purchase. Visa calls it first-party misuse, and Mastercard calls it first-party fraud.

Check the reason code first. For "unauthorized" fraud claims, submit Visa CE3.0 or Mastercard First-Party Trust evidence if the customer qualifies. For "not received" or "canceled" claims, submit delivery proof, usage logs and your cancellation records. For low-value orders, accepting the dispute or refunding on an alert is often cheaper than fighting it.

Partly. 3DS generally shifts liability for fraud disputes to the issuer, so "I didn't authorize this" claims on authenticated payments rarely cost you. It doesn't help with "item not received" or "I canceled" disputes, which need delivery proof and cancellation records.

No. CE3.0 needs two undisputed purchases on the same card made 120 to 365 days earlier, so it only protects returning customers. For first-time buyers, rely on 3DS and standard evidence.

Yes. Mastercard's First-Party Trust program covers reason code 4837 disputes. It needs one device, one delivery and one extra identity data point, and Mastercard checks them against the cardholder's past purchases. The same evidence table you build for Visa feeds both.

It depends on the stage. At checkout, your PSP's 3D Secure and rules engine. After payment, post-purchase screening such as Chargeflow Prevent holds risky orders before they ship. Before a chargeback, Verifi Order Insight and Ethoca Consumer Clarity show cardholders the order details, while Verifi and Ethoca alerts (offered by many PSPs and by Chargeflow Alerts) and RDR let you refund early. After a chargeback, Visa CE3.0, Mastercard First-Party Trust and dispute automation tools submit the evidence. For developers, the Chargeflow API covers the alert and dispute stages across PSPs, and Chargeflow Connect does the same for platforms.

Nvidia's Board of Directors is preparing to oust co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang following revelations of two extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of working for Chinese intelligence and another with an Nvidia executive, reports The Wall Street Journal. Although no final decision has been made yet, the company's directors could meet as early as November 11 to discuss Huang's future. Whoever succeeds Huang will be the company's second CEO in 33 years. Nvidia's stock dropped 8% in after-hours trading following the reports. Nvidia's board of directors launched an independent investigation into the matter on November 8.

The report from the WSJ comes hours after the New York Times revealed that Huang allegedly had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reports directly to him. According to five people who worked at Nvidia, the relationship was known internally, while Huang and Powell were reportedly seen together at a San Jose hotel during Nvidia's GTC conference in March. The allegations follow an earlier report that Huang had a relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese intelligence asset.

A similar controversy cost Intel chief executive Brian Krzanich his position in June 2018, when an internal investigation confirmed that he had maintained a consensual relationship with an employee, which violated the company's non-fraternization policy applicable to all managers. It is noteworthy that Nvidia's code of conduct explicitly identifies personal relationships as potential conflicts of interest and instructs employees to consult the company's legal department when such conflicts arise. Whether Huang violated Nvidia's internal policies remains unclear, as the code of conduct does not explicitly prohibit all relationships between managers and subordinates.

Huang's potential departure would mark the first CEO transition in Nvidia's 33-year history, and therefore his succession has become an immediate concern for Nvidia, which does not have anyone of Huang's caliber in the leadership team. Although chief financial officer Colette Kress could potentially serve as interim chief executive if Huang is ousted while the BoD searches for a permanent replacement, it remains to be seen how Wall Street would react to this assignment.

Nvidia co-founder Chris Malachowsky, who used to be the company's senior vice president of engineering and operations and remains a member of the company's board and an Nvidia Fellow, could also play a role in the succession process, given his extensive knowledge of Nvidia's technology, corporate culture, and history. However, has not served in an executive role at Nvidia for at least a decade, so the chances that he will succeed Huang are low.

Back on Sunday, directors expressed confidence in Jensen Huang and his leadership team, a choice of words that did not exactly guarantee his continued tenure.

#10381. I’ve waited a long time for the Boox Picco, and I’m not disappointed

At around $100, the Boox Picco offers one of the most portable e-reader experiences you can get. You add MagSafe-like capability with a refreshingly simple UI, and you have a delightful way to read, literally wherever you are.

There is an argument to be made for every single shape and size e-readers come in, and they come in so many different sizes it’s hard to keep track. I love the idea of having a 10-inch display that I can skim, but even if it’s perfect for sitting at home and reading anything from novels to comics, I don’t think it provides a very good travel experience

But even smaller devices like the Boox Palma make you choose between bringing a second device or sticking with your phone. Most often, the phone wins out – especially when you have a flexible approach with a foldable like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 I’ve been using daily.

Unlike the other phone-sized e-readers from Boox, the Picco stands at just 4.15 inches tall. The screen measures at just under that – 3.97 inches. It’s essentially the size of a MagSafe or Qi2 wallet – just small enough to fit on the back of your phone with the included magnetic case.

It’s thin, too. A 5.5mm side profile means it slips anywhere a minimal wallet would without issue. That goes for pockets just as well as crossbody bags; perfect for travel.

And that’s where I think I find so much more joy in using this over what would otherwise be considered a small e-reader, like the Palma. I don’t have a lot of excuses not to carry it around when I’m on the go. I’ll throw it in my Bellroy bag when I’m carrying what I’d considered my minimal EDC. It slides into any internal pocket, and it weighs next to nothing.

The back of the Boox Picco isn’t magnetic, but the included case is. If you want the thinnest possible footprint, forego the case. But adding it lets you do one of the coolest – and slightly copium-inducing – things with your phone: attach the e-ink device directly to your OLED-laden phone.

It does not work well with an unconventional device like my Galaxy Z Fold 8, but if you have nearly any other device like the Pixel 11, you should get a rather perfect fit. The Picco squares up to the back of any slab phone with Qi2 magnets, whether internal or via a case.

But, why? Why slap another device and add weight/thickness to your phone when it’s perfectly capable of displaying e-books?

Because it’s cool! That’s the driving reason. You can make the argument that it doubles your phone’s usability or that it gives you an easy place to store the tiny e-reader. The truth is that it does add extra thickness to your phone, and using your phone with the Picco piggybacking along can be uncomfortable, since your fingers now rest on another display and not a case or phone backing.

You can get used to it, and, as unnecessary as it may seem, it’s a fun way to carry around a much more eye-friendly screen.

The Picco diverts from other Boox devices in another way. It doesn’t run Android, which means you have no access to third-party apps like Google Play Books, Amazon Kindle, or any other store/library. Instead, the Picco uses a companion app to transfer EPUBs from your phone to the tiny e-reader.

I initially opposed this idea when I got a sneak peek during IFA in Berlin this year. But after using it for a few weeks, I’ll admit I’ve come around. But that all comes down to how you consume your media.

I try to source EPUBs no matter what device I use. On Android-powered e-readers, that means downloading Google Play Books and reading from there; I have my EPUBs uploaded to my own Google Play Books library, so they’re available universally.

On the Picco, my approach hasn’t changed much. I take those same EPUBs I have in storage and transfer them from the companion app.

I can understand how the lack of third-party libraries would make the Boox Picco moot. Still, I’ve been a proponent of buying digital books I can store in my own drives, so I can read them wherever, whether that’s the Google Play Books library or from a device like the Picco.

All of that is a roundabout way of saying the Picco, though it doesn’t let you use apps to read, makes it easy to get digital copies loaded and ready to flip through.

It uses a handshake connection that requires you to open the companion app on your phone, hit connect, and do the same on the Picco. Once connected, transferring EPUB files is as easy as selecting them from your phone’s physical or cloud storage and queueing them up. The process takes seconds, and the only issue I’ve had was solved by a force stop and trying again.

The homescreen is simply a carousel of your library, with a delightful little progress bar under each title as they’re sorted. You can access and manage the bookshelf from that page, as well as the minimal “apps” and settings. I appreciate the focus app and reading stats, but the countdown and to-do options require using the companion app. I don’t see the point of those.

It doesn’t even have a control panel. Swiping down from the top surfaces screen brightness and color controls. Even though this little guy is just over $100, it still has a front light controlled by a physical switch on the side. Compare that to e-readers at much higher price points without that game-changing feature.

The buttons opposite don’t control volume. Instead, they’re there for page turning.

It’s just simple and well-designed. Features are there to make reading a better experience, down to granular text controls for your digital books. It does exactly what it needs to do – nothing more, nothing less.

As far as battery goes, it meets my expectations. It’s not massive, so the battery is small in comparison to a smartphone. It still holds its own easily, with an easy week of use if you’re reading for an hour or two a day. Beyond that, it takes little time to charge and does great on idle, which is perfect for such a passive device.

The Picco will hit home for you if you want an ultra-portable option for your e-books. The same goes for those who don’t mind the smaller screen and lack of Android or third-party app support.

I get genuine joy every time I pick it up to read where I left off, and I think that’s because it’s so simple and nothing about it feels bloated, even the companion app, which is also straight to the point.

I think it’s been a while since a device has offered that experience for me. Adding the form factor, optional magnetic attachment for your phone, and price tag just gets me to that conclusion sooner.

The Boox Picco is the most adorable e-reader I’ve used, and it’s $109 on Amazon.

#10380. What AI Gets Wrong About the Front End, and Why You Still Need to Know

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

The product carousel looks finished. The image fills the card, the price sits under the product name, and the arrow on the right takes you to the next item. The demo goes smoothly.

Then you put the mouse down. You press Tab, and focus skips the arrows entirely. If you rely on a keyboard, the first product is the only one you can reach.

That’s a front-end bug hiding in plain sight. It’s also a good illustration of where AI fits into front-end development. A prompt can describe what a component should look like and what should happen on click. The implementation still has to account for how people reach that control, activate it, and understand what changed.

Imagine asking an AI coding assistant for this:

Build a React product carousel with previous and next arrows. Show one product at a time and wrap around at the ends.

Here’s an illustrative excerpt from the sort of implementation that can satisfy a quick mouse-driven demo:

With some CSS, this can look exactly like the arrow in the design. The click handler advances the slide. A screenshot shows the right layout.

But a plain div sits outside the normal Tab sequence and has no native button semantics or keyboard activation. Adding tabIndex={0} would make it reachable while leaving Enter and Space behavior to be implemented separately. The browser already provides those behaviors through a native button.

The real omission was in the requirement. “Show arrows” described the visual design. “Let someone reach and operate both controls with a keyboard” describes behavior you can test.

Here’s a small version of the same carousel. The product data is fixed for the example, and the slides change only when the user requests it.

The buttons have visible labels and work with both Enter and Space. When a slide changes, focus stays on the button you pressed, so you can press it again to keep browsing. The status message gives assistive technology a way to announce the new product and its position. Only the current product link is rendered, so Tab never lands on a link from a hidden slide.

Those are deliberate interaction choices. W3C’s carousel pattern provides guidance on using native buttons, keeping focus on the slide controls after activation, and handling automatic rotation when a design requires it. W3C Carousel Pattern

I’d revise the original prompt like this:

Build a manual React product carousel. Use native Previous and Next buttons. Both must work with Tab, Enter, and Space. Keep focus on the activated button after a slide change. Announce the new product name and position through a status message. Keep only the current product link in the Tab sequence. Show what happens when the user advances past the last product.

The extra detail also gives you a review plan. For this carousel, I’d use four checks:

AI can help draft automated tests for the active link and wraparound behavior. I’d still run the keyboard and screen reader checks on the integrated page. A global stylesheet can erase a visible focus outline. A surrounding component can introduce an extra tab stop. The experience depends on the page the customer actually uses.

A checkout form can look complete with sample data and lose the customer’s entries when a request fails. A responsive header can match the design at two widths and overlap when a translated label is longer. A component can render correctly in isolation and shift the page when a slow image loads.

Each example gives AI a concrete job. Ask it to preserve form values after a failed request, check the header with longer labels, or reserve space for the image. Then reproduce the condition yourself. Knowing which conditions matter is part of knowing the front end.

The next time AI gives you a carousel that looks ready, start the review with your hands off the mouse. Tab to Next, press Space twice, and see where focus lands. That short test gives you evidence about how the component works for someone who relies on a keyboard.

The hub now tells the console it’s Nintendo’s own dock.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A hobbyist going by mkopec turned an approximately $45 Cable Matters USB-C hub into a working Nintendo Switch 2 dock, using only about 540 bytes of code to mod the firmware. That mod lets the hub masquerade as an official dock, as mkopec detailed in a blog post. The edited firmware replies to Nintendo’s vendor messages and returns the same identity as the official dock, and makes TV mode work, which was not the case with the hub’s stock firmware. A separate fix with minor firmware rewriting also corrects washed-out HDR over HDMI, a nice bonus.

The modder, who writes that “Nintendo went in a proprietary direction (as they so often do),” decided to modify the hub’s firmware to make a working travel dock, as Nintendo’s official dock can be bulky. Unlocking the additional functionality did not come with a noticeable cost, as the hub “still works normally with my PC and my phone.” Grabbing an off-the-shelf USB-C hub and turning it into something more is quite the trick.

The stock hub has no problem charging the console, but it shows no picture, even though it negotiates both power and DisplayPort Alt Mode. Capturing the official Switch 2 dock’s traffic with a USB Power Delivery (USB-PD) sniffer, the modder found that it advertises two Standard or Vendor IDs: one for DisplayPort and one for Nintendo’s own mode.

The console enters Nintendo’s mode first, then DisplayPort, and, once DisplayPort is configured, it sends Nintendo’s vendor messages. This is the exchange of proprietary messages for negotiation, although the company told us last year that it “does not have any intention to hinder or invalidate legal third-party dock compatibility.”

The modification only required adding about 540 bytes to a firmware of just 32 KiB. The Cable Matters 7-in-1 triple display hub, like most, is simply an amalgamation of separate, specialized chips, in this case: a VL103 as the USB-PD controller, a VL817 USB hub chip for the USB ports, an RTD2142 DisplayPort Multi-Stream Transport chip for the DisplayPort-to-HDMI function, and XT25F16B flash memory chips. The VL chips are from VIA Labs, the RTD2142 is from Realtek, and the stock hub reports VIA’s vendor ID, which is an identity that needed to be changed for this mod.

The modder first used the WITRN K2 inline USB-PD sniffer on the official dock. Then, it was a matter of dumping the VL103’s firmware with the vli plugin of fwupd, the Linux firmware update tool, before flashing the VL103 with the changes over USB and through the VL817.

Changes were made incrementally, with seven versions in all, starting with answers to Nintendo’s discovery, mode entry, and echo commands, then an update to power delivery to offer 15 V at 2.8 A like the dock, changing the reported vendor ID to Nintendo’s, masquerading entirely as the official dock and getting TV mode working, and finally a full sequence match that removed a pause of about 3 seconds.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The process appears to contradict claims two accessory makers made to The Verge that the dock check uses encryption with a dedicated chip, as, in this case, copied identity data and fixed replies were sufficient.

Getting TV mode to work would have already been an accomplishment worth celebrating, but the modder took it further: the picture over HDMI was washed out with HDR turned on, and it was simply a matter of narrowing down the cause. The end theory was a mistake in how the hub’s AVI InfoFrame signaled BT.709, the standard dynamic range color space, instead of HDR’s wider BT.2020.

The theory was confirmed by a 108-byte patch to the RTD2142’s firmware, flashed with flashrom over I2C carried on the DisplayPort AUX channel through the same USB-C cable, which marks the signal as BT.2020 whenever HDR is in use. One third-party dock’s firmware contains a debug string, “switch2 color space patch,” which suggests this is a known issue. HDR through the hub’s own DisplayPort port is still washed out.

Separately, the hub’s firmware has no variable refresh rate (VRR) support, but because the patched hub identifies as the official dock, the console now offers VRR. However, turning VRR on froze the DisplayPort picture, and HDMI remained at 60 Hz. In a separate Linux test, with the hub patched to advertise Adaptive-Sync and an EDID override in place, the screen went black as soon as the frame rate varied, so the feature was left off.

The modder’s post shares no code, patch files, or repository, although the method is well-explained. The USB ports and Ethernet weren't tested rigorously, and the post does not say which Switch 2 system version was used. The modder also doesn’t understand many of Nintendo’s commands, so the hub’s version replies are copies of the official dock’s, and unrecognized commands still get the hub’s stock reply.

That’s important because Nintendo’s system update 21.0.0 left some third-party docks charging but with no video output. While vendors provided updated firmware as a fix, the modder’s ad hoc solution has no vendor behind it, so would-be modders could end up on their own.

#10375. Nintendo will soon discontinue Google and Apple sign-ins

Nintendo Switch users have until January 25 to change how they sign in to the Nintendo Switch app on their smartphones.

Nintendo is going all-in on passkeys in a scheduled update to the Nintendo Switch app and will be sunsetting 3rd party logins after January 25, 2027. The news was made available on an official Nintendo support page. That means you won’t be able to use your Google or Apple accounts to log in to your Nintendo account as of January 26. After January 26:

Instead of using 3rd-party account linking, Nintendo is recommending that users register a passkey for an exclusive, secure login experience through the Nintendo Switch app. If you forget to do this before January 26, you can always head to the Nintendo account page and run through the “forgot password” instructions. Nintendo recommends making sure you can log in to your account ASAP via non-Google or Apple links to ensure that you don’t run into problems before January.

Nintendo didn’t elaborate on the policy change, although some surmise it’s based on security-related measures. The advancement of AI has created bots that can hack into systems with unprecedented speed, so it’s possible that Nintendo is simply trying to shore up any possible area it cannot 100% control. Either way, if you use the Nintendo Switch app or have a Nintendo account of any kind, you should change how you log in immediately.

#10373. Even Realities glasses are coming to a job site near you

Even Realities is making its first big push into the enterprise business world with a new Enterprise SDK release.

Even Realities’ G2 glasses have been a hit for the company, making up 11% of the AR glasses market as of September. Now that consumers are clearly interested in what they can do, Even Realities is branching out to the business world with the release of the company’s first Enterprise SDK (software development kit).

The SDK works well with Even Realities’ app-based software, which lets users browse a bespoke app store filled with games, utilities, and more, all of which are designed to be used on the Even Realities G2’s in-lens displays. In our Even Realities G2 review, reviewer Andrew Romero said the glasses are “for the tech minimalist who wants to stay connected to notifications, while keeping a healthy distance away.”

In the business world, that actually makes a lot of sense. XR glasses and other types of smart glasses with displays are used in fields where you might need more information in front of you but can’t be on a device like a phone. Even Realities glasses are also extremely useful for keeping up with notifications when they come through, something that would be very handy on a job site.

“We built Even G2 to help people access useful information while staying present in their everyday lives, and we believe that principle matters just as much at work. With the Enterprise SDK, we’re giving companies the flexibility to build around the way their teams already work, rather than asking them to change their workflows to fit the technology,”– Will Wang, Founder and CEO of Even Realities

The SDK will allow companies to build custom interfaces, directly integrate glasses’ inputs (microphone and motion data) into apps, and handle other traditional IT management needs like managing device connections and updates. Companies can sign up on the Even Realities enterprise page.

Sony has canceled Fairgames, a heist game announced in 2023, according to Bloomberg. Fairgames had once been part of Sony’s big planned push for PlayStation live service games, but the company ended up canceling some planned live service titles, including in the God of War and The Last of Us franchises, and it shut down Concord shortly after its failed launch.

The Fairgames cancellation won’t result in job cuts, and developer Haven Studios will now support other PlayStation studios, Bloomberg reports. The game was canceled following a recent test where “player feedback and retention results were mixed and fell short of the goals we had set,” according to part of an executive memo published by Bloomberg, which also cited “challenging market conditions in the PVP shooter genre.” Sony acquired Haven Studios in 2022.

Sony’s live service efforts have seen some success with Helldivers 2, which is also available on Xbox. Bungie’s Marathon, which launched this year, has had a rough start, but today the studio showed off some new features coming in a December update, including a new co-op PvE roguelite mode and a PvP deathmatch mode. Sony is also working on a live service Horizon spinoff, but recently rebooted it.

The AI data center boom is bringing hope to struggling cannabis farmers as they face increased competition, costs, and taxes amid reduced demand for marijuana. According to Arizona Public Media, the cannabis industry is in decline, with sales peaking in 2024 and oversupply driving prices down. And now, several growers are considering selling their cultivation facilities or converting them into “mini data center nodes.” These facilities already have many of the ingredients needed for AI data centers, such as the increasingly hard-to-get supply of electricity and water infrastructure.

"For some reason, there's a lot more cannabis grown in Arizona than Arizonans use. And so, a lot of folks are getting out of that business, like myself, at least on the cultivation side. But these facilities can potentially be repurposed to be mini data center nodes," Moe Asnani, the former owner of two Tucson D2 Dispensaries, told the public broadcaster. He also added, "The whole idea is if you create these smaller nodes where people control their own data, where they're not at the mercy of other people's updates and things like that — that's kind of where the idea came in, because I believe in decentralization."

Cannabis farming is both power- and water-intensive. Forbes looked at a 32,850-square-foot cannabis facility in Kalamazoo, Michigan, which is currently wired for 1.5 megawatts, which can be expanded to 2.5 megawatts in under a year and 15 megawatts in the long term. It's also provisioned for fiber internet and equipped with a state-of-the-art HVAC system for climate control, which should make it a tempting property for anyone wanting to put up a small data center — something that even OpenAI and Anthropic are interested in as massive hyperscale sites face opposition from the community.

This concept is dubbed "adaptive reuse," with Tucson City Council member Paul Cunningham saying that it’s a more palatable alternative to massive, purpose-built sites sitting on the outskirts of town. "Data centers are dirty words, and everybody knows that. And no one wants to build a brand-new data center anywhere," the politician said. "But if we have buildings that were using that amount of water and that amount of energy already in their previous function and [it] can be done without being invasive, I'm OK with exploring that option."

There is massive demand for data centers, but it’s not a guaranteed payoff for struggling cash-strapped growers looking to unload their unprofitable properties. Niki Krear, vice president of acquisitions of real estate investment trust New Lake Capital Partners, said that there’s a sweet spot between connectivity, costs, and regulation that data center operators look for in a site.

"It’s a combination of finding affordable power, dense fiber networks, and favorable tax policies," Krear told MJBizDaily. Even though many cultivation facilities already boast higher-than-average power capacity for lighting and climate control, data centers often demand twice to thrice more, with upgrades possibly taking up to five years.

Data center operators looking for smaller sites may also have to contend with NIMBY — not in my backyard — fights from neighbors. Additionally, there may be zoning restrictions, moratoriums, and regulatory hurdles, and the lack of economies of scale could end up costing operators more.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

This is particularly important as AI chips are expected to increase in power and efficiency in the next five years. As these new AI GPUs become available, data centers will need to sell their existing equipment and buy new hardware to remain competitive. Because suppliers usually offer favorable pricing for larger orders, upgrading these smaller sites will likely end up being more expensive on a per-unit basis. That said, growing opposition toward large new projects could make these former cannabis farms suitable alternatives for operators desperate to get more compute online quickly, provided they check all (or most of) the boxes they need.
